paragraphs.text: THE FIRST BOOK OF THE LETTERS OF RURICIUS.
I. RURICIUS TO BISHOP FAUSTUS, HIS SPECIAL LORD IN CHRIST, HIS LORD AND PATRON.

Long ago, my lord, venerable and most blessed bishop, I came to know you through the report of your widespread fame. Long ago, once the longing of a devout love had been poured into me, I began to gaze on you with those eyes of the heart to which you deign to write. Even so, I am eager to see you with my bodily eyes as well. Perhaps then, through your intercession, I might break the chains of my sins, take the wings of that dove and fly away from the hunters' snares, and, settled beside you, rest in the Lord's law. Then, present in person at the source from which your little works flowed, I might drink more deeply and quench the thirst I felt while reading them. Then too the small flame of charity, which you stirred up with your burning sparks in the lukewarm embers of my sleeping soul, might be fed with fuel brought out of the thicket of the Scriptures and grow strong into a living fire. Kindled by the eloquence of your holy mouth, that fire would do what it always does and exert the force of its mighty nature in a sinner's breast, warming what is cold, lighting up what is dark, and burning away the thorns of sin. My soul has clung to you, excellent teacher. May your prayers help me to spurn earthly pursuits and long for heavenly ones. For the body, which is corruptible, weighs down the soul, so that it cannot incline its ear to the divine oracles, forget its father's house, obey the command of the One who calls it, depart from its own land and kindred, and desire instead the land that is shown to it.

Our feebleness is not yet strong enough to drive out the fear that belongs to our guilty condition, or to open hearts purified for perfect charity, so that we might leave present things behind, seek eternal ones, cast out the heir of the slave woman, and obtain our father's inheritance as free men. I therefore hope, my lord, that you will pray for me without ceasing. Whenever you deign to drench the dryness of my land with the rain of your eloquence, please do not serve me delicate and sweet foods, as you have done now while still unaware of my infirmity, but harsher fare suited to my sickness, since luxuries do no good to a fool. And from now on, please give only a censor's assent to those who have told you about me. As human nature goes, they are hampered by excessive affection, turn aside from true judgment, and fall into falsehood out of love. Let Your Holiness have no fear that my wounds would welcome the hand that soothes more than the hand that cuts. By the Lord's gift I already sense that I cannot cure them myself and that they have badly festered. So I choose to have the righteous rebuke me in mercy rather than to have the oil of the sinner anoint my head. With humble entreaty, then, I ask you to draw on that treasure of your inner chambers, from which you are accustomed to bring out things new and old. You are a most skilled physician who, with the help of God's grace, daily heals the countless and varied illnesses of the sick. Send to my sickness as well the medicines you know to be fitting.
II. RURICIUS TO BISHOP FAUSTUS, HIS SPECIAL LORD IN CHRIST, HIS LORD AND PATRON.

Impious negligence and negligent impiety have so far gripped me that I do not know, my lord, what in myself I should accuse first, nor can I find what in myself I should excuse first. If I try to put forward some argument to make excuses for my sins, I shall add sin to sin with no thought of the judgment and crush myself under a double and greater offense. Guilty of tardiness, I would begin to be guilty of falsehood as well, and stretch my offense beyond the merely human wrong. Where I now await only a fatherly sentence for the fault of sloth, I would then fall under God's sentence as punishment for a lie. This is all the more so because a true confession earns indulgence, while a false excuse earns displeasure. So I would rather seek pardon by a confession as simple as it is humble than double my sins.

You have in me, then, best of fathers and excellent shepherd, a voluntary confessor of my fault. In the error of your disciple you have something to correct, and in the sickness of your little sheep something to heal. It is in your power and at your discretion whether you cut away the rot of my ulcer with the hard steel of the knife or cure it with gentle medicines. Whichever cure you choose, I shall embrace it without fear, and I shall not shrink from the blow of a father's hand, so long as I obtain a share of the promised inheritance. I shall not consider what punishment I receive under the lash, but what [?] I have in the testament. It is better for me to weep over a father than to be despised and disowned by a father, because the love of parents chastises in order to correct, not in order to go on punishing. The arrogance of a proud son brings them less grief than the humility of a son who confesses brings them joy.

So that most indulgent father in the Gospel received with a glad embrace the son who had squandered the property he had been granted, readier to rejoice at his return than to reproach him for his fall. His crimes are not thrown in his face, nor his debauchery, nor his destitution. The mere return of the converted son makes up for every loss, for without doubt the means of his return mattered more to the father than the means of his estate. So the son whom departure had made guilty, return made innocent, and mercy is enough for the heir. Indeed, fatherly clemency is not satisfied with pardon alone, with holding him in its arms and soothing him with kindness. It must also heap up generous gifts. The father gives a ring, so that faithlessness may not lead the son away from his father again. He gives shoes for his feet, so that he may more easily scorn the roughness and hardship of the steep road. He gives him the very first robe, the one he had lost, so as to bestow his former immortality on the son he had received back from death. And the younger son on his return is given the calf, which is the same victim that had been given as a lamb to the elder when he was about to set out from Egypt, because it is the same Father who leads them out of Egypt.

Imitate the faithfulness of so great a parent. Extend help to sinners, grant remission to those who strive, bestow your intercession. To a son who confesses, do not only grant pardon yourself, but plead for pardon on his behalf, so that the one you call free in a foreign land you may see set free in his own. And may he who lost the Lord's liberality through his own fault win liberty through you. Let him not be cut off from your comfort, even though he is set apart from the reward.
III. RURICIUS TO HIS MOST DEVOTED SON, THE EVER MAGNIFICENT HESPERIUS.

My lack of skill had blocked the way to writing to you, my kindred spirit, but affection has opened it, together with love, the mistress of all things. Through love, rigid things are bent and stony things softened. The swollen are calmed and the rough made smooth, the smooth swell and the savage grow gentle, the gentle turn savage and the placid are set ablaze. The dull are sharpened, the barbarous gain the upper hand, and the monstrous are tamed. Love has done its work in me too. It has unlocked my tongueless mouth, drawn me out of the safest retreat of silence to face public and fearsome judgment, and forced me in an already old life to take up new things. Until now I followed that ancient maxim which says that it is often better to be silent than to speak, and I preferred to cover my ignorance with modest silence rather than display it shamelessly in uncouth speech. Now, forgetting my habit as much as my rusticity, as if suddenly changed from Arion into Orpheus, I would present myself with chattering mouth to your most eloquent ears, more offensive than dutiful, as I attempt the unknown and venture the unaccustomed.

But you will pardon, I think, one who comes driven by the compelling necessity of close kinship, for a heart that knows the same feeling recognizes what power love naturally claims over the minds of mortals. So let us not linger over excuses and stretch this page until it brings you not only [?] from rough speech but also boredom from disordered abundance. Now we burst out in the voice of affection and pour forth the words of our desires, commending to you our pledge, your trust, by taking charge of whom you have captivated us. To you I have entrusted the hope of my posterity, the comfort of my present life and, if God grants it, the relief of the life to come. To you alone I have committed all my prayers. You I have chosen to draw out and shape precious stones, to search for gold, to find hidden water. You know how to restore to their true nobility gems buried in rock, which in so great a jumble of things would surely lose their worth if no one pointed them out. Gold too, mixed with worthless sand, can keep neither its splendor nor its value unless the craftsman's skill washes it in water and melts it down in fire. And when the veins of flowing water are blocked and the bed of a stream is covered over with earth, the water will not flow unless someone seeking it works hard to clear out the rubble. In the same way, the keenness of still-tender minds, beset by the cloud of ignorance as if by a thick and scaly rust, cannot grow bright by itself unless it is cleaned by a teacher's constant file. It is yours, then, yours now, in all these matters to live up both to your reputation and to our judgment, so that you may not seem to have presumed rashly, nor we to have chosen thoughtlessly.
IV. RURICIUS TO HIS MOST DEVOTED SON, THE EVER MAGNIFICENT HESPERIUS.

I have received your letter, my kindred spirit, sprinkled with grace as much as with eloquence, with love as much as with charm, with salt as much as with honey, so that it lacked neither sweetness nor savor. Though it excels in every art of style and reasoning, it seems to fall short of itself in one thing only, its judgment. My little page deserves no praise and is fit rather for censure because of its clumsy rusticity, yet you hasten to give it more than it deserves. In following either the course of a declaimer or the affection of a friend, you have swerved from the rule of right judgment. I think your excellence came down to this not through any fault of ignorance but by deliberate design, for three reasons: to display, in slender material, the sharpness of your mind, the fluency of your tongue, and the abundance of your speech. On barren and idle ground a farmer's vigor shows all the more, when he tames the resistance of stubborn clods by driving the plowshare through them again and again, or enriches excessive dryness by spreading manure, so that his industry produces the abundance of fruit that the nature of the soil denies. In the same way you have enriched the poverty of my letter with the richness of your eloquence. If you keep it to yourself, it may pass as praiseworthy on your word; but if you make it public, it will bring shame both on me for undeserved praise and on you for an error of judgment. Since you have chosen to stake your own honor on my lack of skill, take care that your choice is not put at risk when we fail to live up to your praise. So if you trust me at all, if you have any regard for both of us, hide away this volume, unworthy of memory and most worthy of oblivion, if you want me to keep, at your discretion, the reputation of an orator, and yourself the standing of a judge of proven worth.
V. RURICIUS TO HIS MOST DEVOTED SON, THE EVER MAGNIFICENT HESPERIUS.

You had promised, dearest son, to send me some little flowers from the young branch you had undertaken to transplant and change from bitterness to a cultivated flavor. By their fragrance I was to learn what hope I ought to hold: whether the flowers promised buds, whether the buds in turn promised fruit by their quality, and whether that fruit could ripen under your care and satisfy the hearts of listeners with the sweet food of eloquence. Since you have put this off, for what reason I do not know, I have found a fitting time to remind you. It is the season when, in the harmony of the world, all living creatures, brute and tongueless alike, those that walk, fly and creep, each in its own way, with its own hisses and its own cries, though with discordant sound and differing voice, yet with equal feeling, burst out as if in one chorus in praise of their own Creator, and show that they feel the power they cannot express. At this season the face of the whole world comes back to life. Whatever in it until now was squalid with neglect, rough with cold, frozen with ice, unsightly in its bareness, or dead before its time from drought, emerges in the likeness of a resurrection. So human frailty may learn to know the invisible from the visible and the future from the present, and may lay aside despair and take hold of the hope of a better age to come. Now too the earth, wedded through hidden channels, has conceived in springtime as if from male seed, and loosens for birth the veins that barren stiffness had kept closed. From this it brings forth everything that is pleasant for delight, sweet to eat, useful for service, necessary for life, pleasing to see, fragrant to smell, and soft to the touch. For this is that mild season which, like a most gentle nurse, held in its lap and nourished the matter of the newborn world while it was still tender and in its cradle, so that the summer heat would not scorch it, nor winter cold extinguish it, nor gusts of wind carry it away while it was not yet hardened by any toil. So your pupil has a most suitable time to renounce at last the sluggishness of his mind and sharpen the dullness of his heart. If he cannot declaim among men, let him at least hasten to cry out among the cattle or chatter among the birds.
VI. RURICIUS TO THE HOLY LORD AND MOST DEVOUT FATHER, THE PRIEST NEPOTIANUS.

I have received the books Your Holiness sent. They are brilliant in eloquence, complete in knowledge, sound in doctrine, and clear in the purity of their faith. Rich in an abundance of sacred testimonies, outstanding in authority and shining with light, they can easily enlighten the minds of the faithful and expose and refute the errors of unbelievers. A very slight taste of them has enticed me rather than refreshed me, and because of the cares of the world I have not been able to eat my fill. When the stomach is burned up by the heat of fever, it neither accepts the foods it once found sweet when they are offered nor misses them when they are taken away. In the same way the mind, worn out by worldly anxieties and cares, does not desire spiritual feasts when they are absent, does not partake of them when they are set before it, and does not taste them when they are poured in.

Though this is my condition, you have still shown the affection of a loving parent and fulfilled the ministry of a solicitous teacher and the duty of a diligent physician by sending suitable medicines to one who suffers from such weariness. Even if through my negligence I cannot regain my health by them, you will still receive a reward from the just Rewarder, who is accustomed to return kind thanks even for the ungrateful. Of these books, then, I have kept one, as you instructed, and sent back the other, which you should know is the work of Saint Hilary, bishop of the city of Poitiers. Since you had told me to, I have taken care to point this out. The one I kept I have arranged to have copied, with your permission, so that what we cannot commit to memory we may at least take care to commit to the page.
VII. RURICIUS TO BISHOP BASSULUS, HIS SPECIAL LORD IN CHRIST AND PATRON.

In many ways you prove how much your holy devotion and devout holiness deigns to love me. You send things for me to read and correct what I have neglected, you call forth love by loving, and you teach by example what you preach in words. But your seed does not thrive in barren and thorny ground, since the brambles grow over it and choke it. So, lest the lord of the vineyard order me cut down like that unfruitful fig tree, for which he has waited so long in vain, put off the harsher sentence by your prayers, until the richness of your teaching, like manure, sweetens my fruitless bitterness. But since my sins outnumber my words, and I cannot atone for deeds with speeches, I at least pay you the service of a letter. I let you know that I have returned the book you had lent me, and I hope you will likewise have another of yours sent to me by the bearer of this letter, if you no longer need it. And if by God's favor you are coming to Gourdon for the feast of the saints, let me know by the returning messengers.
VIII. RURICIUS TO BISHOP SIDONIUS, HIS SPECIAL LORD IN CHRIST, HIS LORD AND PATRON.

I remember often hearing you preach that we can in no way be cleansed of our iniquities unless, pricked by conscience, we confess our sins. Who could even seek indulgence, let alone obtain it, without joining confession of the error to lament for it? It is error that calls for indulgence, not indulgence that calls for error. Knowing this to be very true, I have not delayed in revealing to Your Devotion a misdeed I recently committed, so that what now leads to pardon because I disclose it may not later become a matter of guilt because I kept silent. So let us bring the trick itself into the open. I declare myself guilty of theft against you, and I confess that I have unlawfully helped myself to your deposit without your knowledge. Yet it was you who gave me the opportunity to commit the crime, whether you were testing a greedy man or wishing to instruct an unlearned one. I confess that I copied the book you had told me to collect from my brother Leontius. If you approve, acknowledge it; if you hold it against me, forgive it, for my confession comes with a complaint. First my own will drove me to read it, and then the book itself forced me to copy it. When I had sampled only a little of its dishes, it so enticed me with the taste of its alluring flavor that, imitating in a way our first parent, I suddenly despised my lord and was bent on eating my fill, heeding the counsel of the tempter rather than the command of the master. To reveal all the secrets of my heart, I seemed to hear the words of the book itself urging me: "Why do you hold back, ungrateful man? Why do you hesitate? You know the will of our common lord toward you, how he strives on various occasions to polish you, how the good shepherd is accustomed to press spiritual food on you even against your will. Believe me, he will hold it against you more if you delay than if you copy, for he is accustomed to favor the studious, not to begrudge them." With these and similar appeals from a silent speaker I threw myself into its chains, both willingly and under compulsion, and hurried to copy it. Whether I should now return it as it is, having copied it, or put in order [?], depends on your decision. I shall gladly accept whatever penalty you impose, for I believe your decree to be my remedy, and I count your sentence a cure, not a punishment.
IX. RURICIUS TO SIDONIUS, HIS SPECIAL LORD IN CHRIST, HIS LORD AND PATRON.

Your Devotion's recent preaching and long-standing love have so enticed me that I dare to wrong your ears quite often with my foolishness, as I long to attain your learning, as far as my barren little wit allows. Though it is a great and difficult thing to reach it, it is nevertheless a fine and noble thing to pursue it, since not only the attainment of the highest things but even their imitation deserves praise. Hardly anyone is left wholly without a share in what he has striven to climb toward and reach. So I long, my lord, I long, I say, to be refreshed with your food, to drink from your fountain, to be filled with your dishes, to grow fat at your banquets. When you serve them, suppose a guest does not merely sip them with the tip of his lips, but eagerly swallows them with all the depths of his soul, then hides them in the inmost part of his heart to chew over later. He will begin to burst out with constant belching in praise of almighty God, his heart full and his mouth fasting, hungering while sated and sated while hungering, to be sated more fully in the regeneration. Nor can that food ever run short whose nourishment lies in the Word. So that I may deserve to share in these delights, win this for me by your patronage. Come to my aid as I strive beyond the measure of my strength. Pray also that I may not be found a stranger to the fold entrusted to you, and carry the straying sheep back from the pastures of the world to the Lord's sheepfolds. For I trust that through your intercessions one who has earned the right to be your disciple may become a lamb.
X. RURICIUS TO HIS LORD LUPUS, HIS DEAREST HEART.

I have received the letter from Your Magnanimity in which you deign to explain that it is the lack of a carrier that makes you sprinkle me so rarely with the dew of your eloquence. You also say you wonder why I decline to write to you more often, since I have plenty of carriers at hand and no lack of elegant, abundant words either. I have no doubt you tossed this off in irony, as befits your witty eloquence, since you have carriers in abundance and you know that I labor under a poverty of speech and the barrenness of a meager talent, like a spring in the summer months that is drying up and seeps rather than flows. You added that you ought to be joined to me as Patroclus was to Achilles, Theseus to Hercules, or Pirithous to Theseus. From these stories and deeds of the ancients we should take not the rank of the persons but a comparison of their love. Recalling the names of these friends, let us follow their examples. Transferring their names to ourselves, let us match their merits. Picking out whatever is magnificent and honorable in their deeds, let us fit it usefully to our own lives, and serve one another with sincere charity, not painted flattery. Let us strive so that what the poets falsely invented in those friendships, the truth of our souls may achieve in us. Then, while we seem to imitate the ancients, we shall leave behind something for others to imitate, and as we praise the deeds of our elders we shall be praised by posterity. These lines, then, my lord, flame of my heart, I have dictated briefly and in haste because the bearer was in a hurry, trusting more to your persuasion than to my own judgment of myself. If your skill and integrity have any regard for a friend's modesty, they will have to either hide them or take care to correct them.
XI. RURICIUS TO HIS SUBLIME AND EVER MAGNIFICENT LORD AND BROTHER FREDA.

Since you wished the trifles of our wilderness to be added to the loveliness of your grove, I have sent, as you instructed, fir saplings. They will please not by their looks but by their height. They are remarkable not for fruit but for having come from far away, and are fit not for use but for charm. Once they have taken root, the thickness of their shade will give the ocean shore the cool of the Cévennes in summer. They will stand among those splendid trees of every kind, outstanding in beauty as much as in usefulness, rich with their burden, bright with flowers, fragrant with scent. For there your diligence has brought together what the nature of the soil did not produce. I pass over the red of the roses, the white of the lilies, the unfading green of the laurel and other such sights, since precious things often grow cheap through abundance and daily plenty breeds distaste. But foreign delights of grasses, shoots and shrubs have also been gathered there, flourishing both for the eye and for use.

But what should be praised or admired first in a place where even the harshness of the seasons is softened? There the heat of scorching summer is driven off by the coolness of both shade and water. The harshness of winter is felt so little that, for those inside, the mild air and the song of birds give the very likeness of spring. But why, my lord, do I forget my lack of skill and strive with poor words to describe or recount the riches and delights of your estate, when even greater talents would fail to praise it? Pardon, then, my impudence, which you yourselves extorted, for your kindness compels me to be wordy in your ears. I trusted that a longer letter, my lords, would please you by its affection even if its style displeased you, since you would understand that it was long not for the charm of eloquence but out of love for you. I also knew that your highness finds more fault in friends who are bashfully silent than in those who are talkative and bold in their familiarity.
XII. Ruricius to Celsus, lord of his heart.

I tremble to open my tongueless mouth in your praise, for I know that even greater talents rightly fail before it. What should I mention first in praise of your affection or your kindness? You have given me all the delights of the countryside, of good manners and, greater than all these, of love. If any of these was lacking, it should be put down to the season, not charged to us. For with you I found everything that a loving heart holds dear and everything the world counts illustrious. You cheated me of no pleasure at all. Indeed, by being my neighbour you have even made the wilderness of my little lodging desirable to me. So I rejoice all the more to live near you, because a man joined to the good is not wholly bad.

But lest a longer speech bore you with its clumsiness, I send you my warmest greetings. I also let you know that I have sent the glassworker, as you ordered. May our affection imitate his work in its brightness, not its fragility. The love left to us by our parents, handed down by our teacher and strengthened by a shared life should be polished by good fortune, and no storm or whirlwind of adversity should ever break it. Consider the precious purity of gold and silver. If it has been corrupted by an admixture of bronze or lead or any other baser material, and is not purged by the testing of fire, it can have neither its natural brilliance nor its ring. It gives no clarity to the eye and no ringing to the ear. Instead it sounds hoarse when struck, and shrill … [?]

So, best of brothers, let us both look to this saying, which is not mine but the Lord's, and follow it. Let us steer our life on a middle course, with the Lord himself as our helmsman. The calm may smile on us, a favourable breeze may beckon, the gentle sea may flatter us. Yet we know that the level surface of the water beneath us can suddenly rise up like mountains. So let us never allow our ship to be driven out into the deep, where a storm may break it apart or a wave may sink it.
XIII. Ruricius to Celsus, lord of his heart.

I have received your brotherly letter, and it has caused me no small worry. I fear that you have taken my little letter in a sense other than the one in which I sent it. You seem to charge me with rash presumption, as it were, when you ask me to pray for you and to remind you more often. Would I dare to rebuke you, best of brothers, when I cannot rebuke myself? Would I rebuke you, who look down as if from a loftier watchtower or a higher hill on me, still tossed about in the whirlwinds of the world like a frail skiff on the surging sea? Would I rebuke you, who [?] to the harbour of pardon through the mercy of penance, with the Lord as helmsman? I did not write at all, dear brother, to flatter myself and bite you with a malicious tooth, nor to hurt you. I wrote to bind you to me by the intimacy of a letter. If you consider it carefully, those words express wishes, not deeds. They are the words of someone hoping rather than admonishing, for I described not how we were acting but how I would like us to live. Besides, if you were to examine the deeds of my past and present life, you would be ashamed to hear, with your closest and most intimate brother as witness, things that I was not ashamed to promise with God as witness. I hope you will rather pray to the Lord for these sins of mine. He willed us to be partners in friendship and kinship in this world; may he command us to share in good things in the world to come.
XIV. Ruricius to Celsus, lord of his heart.

I have sent a horse such as you asked for. He is gentle and calm, sound of limb, firm and strong, handsome in appearance and well built. He is even-tempered, neither too hasty in his speed nor sluggish (in his slowness), and his rider's will serves him as both bridle and spur. He has both the will and the strength to carry a load, so that he neither gives way under his rider nor throws off what is placed on him. Having made this known, as was proper, and having first sent our greetings, we now claim the fulfilment of what you promised [?]. We ask that, God willing, you come to us with your sister for the feast of the saints, to give honour to the patrons, affection to the brethren and favour to the people.
XV. Ruricius to Bishop Aeonius, his own special lord in Christ the Lord, and his patron.

When I learned of the passing of my lord Leontius, your predecessor, whose memory I hold holy and venerable, I was troubled in heart and mind, and I grieved long and deeply. My sins had kept me from deserving to meet so great a bishop, and now I had lost such a father. Although I never enjoyed the sight of his outer man, I delighted in the grace of his inner man and clung to him constantly with the eye of the mind. Through it and in it he was somehow present to me: I saw him with my gaze, heard him speak, touched him and held him in my embrace. Loved ones see each other in no better place than in the heart, the very seat of love. That is why I longed all the more to see with bodily eyes the man I beheld in this way with spiritual ones. But his merits, which had earlier given me comfort, have now consoled my grief. I trust that he whom a father's love cherished will also guard me with his diligent intercession.

I told these things to your holiness at love's prompting, as if I were talking with you and seeking from you some relief for that grief. Now, as I had begun to say, when I learned that my lord had been called away and that you had been ordained to your apostolic office, I was planning to send greetings to you in your new office. But your gifts came before my humble respects could reach you, and they have given me greater confidence in writing. I presume that you do not hold as a stranger to your heart someone whom your generosity has made worthy. You give me to understand that you deign to hold me in such esteem, and so I send your beatitude abundant greetings by letter. At the same time I ask you with special earnestness to deign to treat me with such affection that I may know that lord Leontius has been sent ahead of us and exchanged for you, rather than lost.
XVI. Ruricius to Sidonius, who sees: his venerable lord and admirable brother, worthy to be ranked with all the saints.

Long ago, dearest brother, I came to know you through the widespread fame that proclaims you. In the seat of love I beheld you with the eyes of the mind, the very eyes with which you yourself look down on earthly things more clearly and contemplate the heavenly and divine. That is why I have added to your name the name of that gift with which I saw you endowed. As I gaze attentively at you in the mirror of my heart and greatly admire the beauty of your inner man, you have stirred the depths of my soul to longing. They have been moved to such affection for you, with the purest love, that I desire to see with bodily eyes the man I contemplate with spiritual ones. So, with warmest greetings in Christ the Lord, I ask most especially that you go to the trouble of visiting our lowliness together with my lord the bishop, who I trust will come to us out of his kindness. Then, being together, we may each draw profit from the other's presence. The questioner's eager inquiry becomes the instruction of the one who answers, and in a way both learner and teacher make progress together. Peace, peace, peace.
XVII. Bishop Ruricius to Abbot Pomerius, lord of his soul, to be cherished in Christ the Lord with all the depths of love.

It is written, as you yourself know better than I: "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." So if you hold anything against me, forgive me now, for you should know that the Lord has already avenged it. Know that we were led along such trackless ways into such hidden wilds that the soul shudders to retrace them, the mind recoils from them, and words cannot describe them. We came upon a path blocked with branches and narrow in width. It bristled with thorns, was shut in by stumps and overgrown with briars. It was rough with decay, obstructed by heaps of rocks, paved with tangled roots and a quagmire of mud. Amid such varied and manifold evils the danger took no single form, for the strong roots held back the horses' feet and the rotten soil would not bear them. The path rose so high into the mountains and plunged so deep into the valleys that we felt as if we were sailing a billowing sea stirred up by the blasts of raging winds, with the daylight snatched from our eyes by mists and clouds. Even if the sun's rays shone on the world, their brightness and warmth could not reach us through the density of the forest. All along the way the tall, wretched ferns pressed in on us, and floods of dew so drenched us that, shrivelled and driven by the cold, we sought the warmth of a great fire in the dog days of summer.

But when we reached the place we had been making for, we were surrounded by water and soaked through, and yet we began to die of thirst. As I said, there was a chill in the air, but the spring was lukewarm, the river smelled, the fields were hot and the fort was stifling. To sum it all up briefly: know that we travelled by a road that no one would want to take even to paradise, let alone into exile. Our Lord ordered that I should run into all these things and that you should escape them, distinguishing my sins from your merits even by a visible journey. You, who travel the narrow and laborious way in the spirit, were not to pass through the straits of this one. We, who walk the broad and spacious way, always looking back, were to suffer its injuries. Therefore pray to the Lord, for whom we confess that all things are possible, that even by different roads he may bring us together in one city. Mercy can bring us into it, and merits you.
XVIII. Bishop Ruricius to his sweetest and like-minded son Ommatius.

My not writing to you, my sweet son, by Venerius was due not to negligence or any grievance but to being busy. So I have given this letter to Amelius. With it I send you warmest greetings and urge you always to remember your resolve. Your soul is already dedicated to God, so do not let a more alluring sight call it away from the path you have begun. Do not let more melodious sounds corrupt it, or sweeter tastes taint it, or softer touch tempt it, or more pleasant smells entice it, and so let death enter the soul through the windows of the body. Nor should you look back, against the Lord's word, while holding the plough, so that the furrow loses its straight line. Rather, yearn with all your senses for him to whom you vowed yourself at his own inspiration, and cling to him with your heart fixed on him. Then, when any enticing form of the vices I have named knocks at your door, it cannot approach a heart fortified by firm faith and meditation on God. However much you may seem to be surrounded by crowds, enter the chamber of your heart, shut your door, and do not cease to pray to the Lord. Then he who sees in secret may say to you what he said to holy Moses, who cried out to him not with his voice but with his heart: "Why do you cry to me?" I hope that in such prayers you will deign to remember me too. Even if our affection does not bring you back, may the longing for sweet and wholesome quiet soon bring you to us.
THE SECOND BOOK OF THE LETTERS OF RURICIUS
I. Ruricius to his exalted lords Namatius and Ceraunia, brother and sister to him, most closely bound to him in Christ the Lord.

The wise men of old said that two friends have one soul, and I declare and prove that this is very true. Since I left you, my brother and sister, I feel divided. I know that part of me has stayed behind with you, and while you are away I do not seem whole to myself. Since I cannot find myself in myself, I return to you and look for myself with you. There I see that I carried away as much of you as I left of myself with you. And so, before the hoped-for union of our children takes place with the Lord's consent, a division of souls has already taken place between us. Those who love should embrace this division rather than avoid it, for through it a pure, undivided love flows from heart to heart. I rejoice that you have bound me with its bonds. I exult in such chains and would rather be held fast by their knots than set free, and I trust that you are bound by them too. So I send you my warmest greetings on your return. I give you thanks for everything, but I leave aside anything that touches on your praise. Let me explain why I have kept silent: as the saying goes, boasting of one's own merits is odious. Your praise has become mine. That is why, as I said, I thought it better to keep silent about your magnanimity, because whatever I say about you I seem to be bestowing on myself.
II. Ruricius to his exalted lords Namatius and Ceraunia, brother and sister to him, most closely bound to him in Christ the Lord.

Among the other thanks I rightly owe you, I give you enormous thanks for the presence and visit of our common patron, lord Postuminus. You caused our little lodging to be made bright by his prayers, for in showing us his faith he gives us his blessing. He was a most vigilant inspector, a most insistent collector and a most strict executor. Yet in view of your kindness and the weight of his holiness we counted all this as mild, for, as it is written, "love bears all things; love never fails." Above all, we believe that what he seemed to demand from us he actually brought to us by God's kindness. So now that he is returning, by divine favour, I have given him this letter. It was not needed, but he wished it. With it I send my warmest greetings and my longing to you, my brother and sister, who are one and undivided. In my mind I am already making my journey and seeing you. I also inform you that everything has been inspected, handed over and confirmed, as you instructed and as was fitting and due. Nor do I fear that it should trouble you even a little that one entry seems to have been removed from the dowry document. You will recognize that what is lacking in number has been not only made up but even increased in merit.
III. Ruricius to his exalted lords Namatius and Ceraunia, brother and sister to him, most closely bound to him in Christ the Lord.

Because of our mutual love you can more easily guess than I can express in a letter how heavily I was struck by the dreadful news of your bereavement. A mind worn out with excessive grief refuses to set down what it shudders to recall. I grieve, my most dear brother and sister, at so bitter a blow, and I suffer with you with all my heart. Although for the present I am separated from you in body, I am always joined to you in mind. Since I do not depart from you in spirit, I believe that I am present at your laments, for according to the divine saying, when one member of the body suffers, all the members suffer with it. We are not only made one body by faith in Christ but also linked by the union of our children. So if such harsh weather had allowed it, I would have come to console you myself instead of sending letters.

But what are we to do, my dear brother and sister? We cannot resist the divine command by our strength, and we ought not to resist it by our will. We must guard with all vigilance lest, while we weep with excessive grief for our sweet children, we be found blasphemous or in some way offensive toward the Lord. Then the author of death himself would seize his opportunity and pierce our soul more grievously than he struck it with the loss of our loved ones. So in every bitterness and grief we must flee to him who heals the wounded, lifts up the sorrowful and consoles the afflicted, and we must bring all our misfortunes before him with all our heart. Above all we must say those words of holy Job: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord." I have ventured to write these things to you, lords of my heart, to temper somehow, at least with the words of Scripture, the grief we share, for I knew that my own words could not soften it. And truly you can draw no small comfort from Christ's will. Since an untimely death awaited your son, Christ deigned to take him up as one of those to whom, he said, the kingdom of heaven belongs. So you may have a patron in your son, and grieve less for the one you have lost, since you saw him taken up by the Lord.
IV. Ruricius to his exalted lords Namatius and Ceraunia, brother and sister to him, most closely bound to him in Christ the Lord.

Dearest brothers, I have often resolved to write to you, or to come to you, because of the bitter blow of our shared grief. But each time I have been held back: from setting out on the journey by bodily weakness, and from the duty of writing by the excessive sorrow of my heart. Whenever I tried to bend my mind to writing, my senses at once shuddered and my mind shrank back, and weeping always came to me in place of words, so that I would drench the page with a shower of tears before I could mark it with the pen. As the poet said, describing a father's love at the loss of his son:

“Twice he tried to shape his fall in gold; twice the father's hands dropped.” Or, as I would rather say, “my soul refused to be comforted.” And not without reason. For I have lost a daughter, whom I rejoiced that I had received and you had begotten. I have lost the comfort of my life, the hope of posterity, the glory of the family, the joy of my heart, the light of my eyes. Nor was I struck by a single bereavement. Along with the daughter I also lost brothers, in whose affection I found comfort and in whose bond I took pride. The tie of our kinship has been broken, dearest brothers; the pledge of our mutual love has been taken from you. Alas, best of brothers! In losing what you entrusted to me, by whose giving you had won me, I have lost you as well; and so in the loss of a single relationship I groan that the comforts of many relationships have been taken from me.

Only the homeland that I gained through her I shall not lose, for I shall count above all as my homeland this land which she has taken possession of with her body. But where am I going, forgetful of my duty and mindful only of my love, driven on by grief? Why am I tearing open, with a revived memory as with a fresh incision, a wound that time had partly closed over, and why can I, who wanted rather to comfort you with God's promises, not take comfort myself? Let me explain to you the causes of this relapse of grief. My mind, worn out with sorrow, had somehow begun to accept the comfort of the apostle's exhortation, where he says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who are asleep, so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.” But when our unhappy son, whom we share, arrived, and I saw him without that jewel with which he used to shine, which made him both more welcome and more dear to me, he seemed to me as if stripped of his proper ornament and robbed of his beauty. He who searches the secrets of hearts knows, dearest brothers, that my grief was suddenly doubled, and that day by day my affection and my mourning are doubled, for her fine nature and for his desolation, so that I can neither look at him nor remember her without tears, and I often repeat the prophet's words: “Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” But he was weeping for the sins of his people, while I weep for my own, which have crushed both me and you by their weight and number; I weep so that I may lament her death and my life, her departure and my survival.

You presumed something far different, venerable sister, as if relying on our merits, when, deceived by excessive love, you promised yourself so much from our prayers, though I protested, that you believed your household would be saved by our intercession and your daughter would, so to speak, be made immortal through me. But my merits quickly showed themselves: they have wounded me with an incurable wound, and they have struck you, who believed otherwise than you should have about a sinner, with the loss of so precious a pledge. Now at least, venerable sister in Christ the Lord, you will recognize that you believed what was false and I spoke what was true. But for too long, forgetting the heavenly commandments, we have been giving way to human grief. We must return to God's commandments, so that we do not mourn her dead in body in such a way that we ourselves die in heart. Let us therefore withdraw a little from present things and think again of the things to come, so that the future may strengthen those whom the present weakens. We ought, dearest brothers, to bear that condition of human frailty which the prophets and apostles and all the holy and righteous, and, what is greater, the Lord of all himself, deigned to take on. It is fitting for us to mourn, but even more to give thanks to God and to rejoice that we had such a daughter as we wished for as long as he who gave her allowed, and that we have not lost her as she was when we wished for her, but have sent her ahead to Christ at his own command. To have children is a common blessing, but to have good children is a special reward; just as living is common to all, but to live well and to depart well from this life belongs to few, not because of the condition of nature but because of guilt, not by divine decree but by one's own will.

So let our heart not be troubled, and let us weep for our daughter not as lost but as longed for, so that we may not seem either to disbelieve the Lord's promises or to resist his commandments. Let those weep for their children who cannot have the hope of resurrection, which their own faithlessness has taken from them, not God's sentence. Let the dead weep for their dead, whom they think have perished forever; let those have no rest from their grief who do not believe that there is rest for the dead. But we, whose hope and portion is Christ, our hope in the land of the dying, our portion in the land of the living, for whom this death is the end not of our nature but of the present life, because we believe it will be restored to something better, according to the apostle's words, “when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption,” must say with the prophet: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord.” For penitence must be held fast in temptation, so that temptation does not drive us to sin in either mouth or heart.

Let ready faith, then, wipe away our tears, for we believe that our loved ones do not so much lose life as change it: they leave a world full of hardships and sorrows and hasten to the land of blessedness; they come out of a toilsome exile and arrive at the homeland of rest. This is why the prophet says: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name.”

Believe me, dearest brothers, she is already secure in her own rest and is concerned for our salvation. If she could speak with us, she would say this: “Do not, loving parents, do not weep for me, and do not show yourselves ungrateful to so kind a Lord by the lamentations of excessive love. Granted that affection had this right at the time I was called away; now faith ought to temper your grief with time, for though I am dead to you, I live to God. Can you love me more than the Lord, who made me as he willed, redeemed me because he willed, and received me when he willed, out of his own kindness? Or what greater comfort for your grief can you have than that our Lord deigned to hand over his only Son to death for us? And when the Son of God willed to die according to the flesh, should a human being accept the condition of human lot so bitterly? Therefore, most loving parents, weep rather for your own sins and think about making amends for your offenses, so that, if you love me in Christ (for you cannot truly love me unless you love me in the Lord), you may be worthy to come into the bosom of the patriarch, where the Lord has placed me because of the purity of my innocence and because of his own kindness, for his mercy is better than life, so that there we may rejoice together in joys that are not false but true, not temporal but eternal.”

With such words, best of brothers, and with commandments and promises of the Lord like these, we ought to console ourselves. Just as with the Lord future things are already done, so the faithful Catholic ought in some way to have as already present the heavenly promises which he trusts will be fulfilled in their time: to grasp them by hope, possess them by faith, and secure them by works. For these are what give us comfort in sorrow, confidence in adversity, and moderation in prosperity, so that we are neither lifted up by good fortune, nor give way before adversity, nor are consumed by sadness.

These things, then, dearest brothers, I have dictated, not without great sorrow of heart, to be sent to you for our shared consolation. It was not an abundance of words that made me draw out my discourse somewhat at length, but the turmoil of our hearts, so that long and repeated recollection might soothe the longing that memory had kindled. And in this let us also show equal love toward our common daughter, so that, just as her life bound us together, her memory may keep us in the same love.
V. Ruricius to his exalted lord and most devoted brother in Christ the Lord, Namatius.

We who seek occasions to write as the bond of our kinship requires ought not to let one slip when it is offered, so that the word, acting as go-between, may give us back some share of each other's presence. It is sent out and not lost, given and still kept; it seems to depart and does not go away; it is sent by me and received by you, written by me and read by you, and yet it is not divided, since, though seemingly divided, it is held whole in the heart of each of us. For like the divine Word, it is handed on without going out, conferred on the one in need without being taken from its author: gain to the receiver without loss to the giver, enriching the poor without impoverishing the owner.
VI. Bishop Ruricius to his lord and especial patron in Christ the Lord, Bishop Chronopius.

In ordering or governing the Lord's flock, there ought to be among watchmen and overseers not presumption but reason, and care for guarding, not contention over encroachment, so that they may not incur the mark of hirelings by failing to keep the discipline of shepherds, and may not be found, as the apostle says, seeking not Christ's glory but their own, preferring to receive praise from men rather than to await reward from the Lord, eager for present gain and scornful of eternal reward. Therefore, as the same apostle teaches, if we are of one mind in a peaceful fellowship for the holy work, if we love without pretense, if we minister with diligence, if we are members of one head, we ought to be rulers of the body with one accord. For the folds of the Lord's flock may be many in number, but they are not divided by any difference of faith; so that, as the Lord himself deigned to foretell, no manifold schism may arise through us as we quarrel out of envy and divide the Lord's flock by dissension, but rather, as we gather the Lord's sheep through the unity of simple teaching, there may be in us one flock and one shepherd, who, just as he is King of kings and Lord of lords, Priest of priests and Pontiff of pontiffs, may also be understood to be Shepherd of shepherds. For this reason, out of zeal for love and not out of greed, I have sent this letter to Your Holiness by my priest concerning the parish of Gemiliacum, about which I had already written to you some time ago, so that, if I had kept silent, it would not be put down to negligence rather than to harmony, and I would not seem to have given way to an unreasonable claim rather than to peace. So, if you recognize that what I say is true and what I claim is just, do not allow me to suffer injury, or yourself disquiet, any longer.
VII. Bishop Ruricius to his exalted and ever magnificent lord and brother, Elaphius.

By God's favor the fame of your works has spread so widely that all who are in hardship beg with every kind of entreaty to be commended to Your Brotherliness, for they have no doubt that their trouble will find relief with you. So the bearer of this letter, named Ulfila, whom the priest Pharetrius commended to me in his letter, asked me for a letter of commendation to you, which I gladly granted him, both at God's bidding and at our mutual bidding. In it I send my warmest greetings to your undivided love, and I have presumed to commend the aforesaid man out of brotherly affection, not by episcopal authority. For in a sinner dignity loses its dignity, and undeserved honor is a burden to him rather than an honor. Although I trust that this pleases you because of our close bond, still, if you bear me any true or answering love, I hope you will grieve with me rather than rejoice, for so great an office does not raise me up, unworthy and wholly undeserving as I am, but weighs me down.
VIII. Bishop Ruricius to his holy and apostolic lord, to be honored by me beyond all others in Christ the Lord with especial reverence and affection, his patron and pope, Aeonius.

Whenever those weighed down by a mass of hardships are compelled to seek out holy and apostolic men, whom works of mercy, the merits of those works, and a life worthy of those merits commend, and whom the fame of all virtues spreads abroad, then, while they seek the comfort of a letter for their trouble, they confer a favor on our desire. And though their trouble is our sorrow, their need nevertheless becomes in some way our love through the performance of this duty, for in granting their request we satisfy our own wish; and so it comes about that the need of the one who asks is the benefit of the one who gives. So I have gladly granted a letter of commendation to Your Apostleship to our brother and fellow priest named Possessor, a possessor, what is worse, in name rather than in means, for he poured out everything he had for the ransom of his brother. He has become a possessor of paradise by ceasing to be a possessor of worldly property. If Your Holiness deigns to learn of his need more fully, please consider it worthwhile to read the letter which our brother Bishop Eumerius sent to my lowliness by him, and there you will learn how you ought both to help him according to custom and to sympathize with him out of mutual love. To set his brother free from the enemy, he chose to become captive to his creditors, and so that his brother might not be deprived of life by a most cruel death, he himself became an exile from his homeland.

Considering the words of the holy apostle Paul, where he says in writing to the Romans, “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you, but have been prevented until now,” we too are driven by shame to say: we have often wanted to send letters to Your most sincere Piety, but we have been prevented until now, no doubt by him who is always accustomed to oppose a good will, begrudging, of course, both our progress and your affection, our affection and your progress. Our progress and your affection, because your teaching is our instruction and our letter is a fulfillment of your desire; and again your progress and our affection, because our instruction is your reward, and the brief fulfillment of your desire is the affection of our words. For in those few days, which your affection made truly few and very short for me, since my gaze could not be satisfied by looking at you but rather burned the more by seeing you, so that we longed for you while you were present and still sought you while you were before our eyes, you watered our senses from the purest fountain of your kindly heart, so that, even if I should never again receive the precious gifts of your holy mouth, I still possess your presence within the secret places of my mind and behold your likeness in the mirror of my heart. Love has painted it there so perfectly that no oblivion of any age can erase it, for it is renewed at every moment by constant remembrance.

There, as is your loving custom, I converse with you more privately; there I also discuss the ordering of a better life; there I kiss you with the lips of my mind and embrace you with the hands of my heart. So it is that the true love which is nourished in my inmost being by the living image of your face, and kindled by the spark of charity, promises me in return your love, and my own heart stands surety to me for yours, when I ask my heart, which knows our mutual love, how much I may presume about you. Now that, through your prayers, the way to write has at last been opened to me, I send you greetings in this letter and ask your intercession for my sins, begging this with special entreaty: that you implore the mercy of our God with constant petitions that, when all my [?] have been blotted out and all my offenses forgiven with your help by his customary clemency and abundant goodness, he may bid us come, if not to the same reward, at least to the same harbor of rest; so that, since here, because of the distance of land between us, we cannot often see each other with the eyes of the body, we may at least rejoice there in each other's presence; and that, when the crown of merits is rendered to you by the just Judge, pardon for my offenses may not be denied me by the most loving Redeemer and most perfect Advocate.

May he himself deign to plead the sinner's cause before the judgment, so that he may not punish the guilt at the judgment; for the Almighty knows how neither to lose the truth of judgment in the goodness of his clemency, nor to lose the goodness of clemency in the severity of judgment. And so, by the ineffable working of his mercy and power, may he deign to grant you that those whom he has joined here in truth he may not separate there in their dwelling. Recalling your promise, I ask especially that Your Holiness not only refrain from keeping back brother Pomerius, but even urge him to come to us, and send us his part, inseparable from both of us [?]. And do not think that he is leaving you if he comes to me, for he will find you here in me, and while you remain behind in body, you will, we trust, come with him in heart. Moreover, you will be able to reap no small fruit from it if our rusticity makes some progress in the fear of God through his teaching.
X. Bishop Ruricius to Abbot Pomerius, lord of his soul, to be cherished with his inmost heart in Christ the Lord.

The wise men of this world have said that two friends have one soul, and I confirm that this is true by the testimony of the Church as well, where it says: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul”: one, of course, in love, not in number, and in the simplicity of faith, not in being a single person. This, then, I proclaim and attest. For ever since I left Your Unanimity, I feel that I am divided, and I know that part of me has stayed behind with you. I do not believe that I am whole while you are absent, and since I do not find myself in myself, I return to you and look for myself with you, and there I see that I have carried away as much of you with me as I left of myself with you. And I give thanks to almighty God for so wonderful a work of his, that he has deigned to grant by his universal providence that, between those whom distances of place separate, the mind should pass freely to and fro, confined by no laws of absence, and that nothing should be so impenetrable as not to lie open to the gaze of the mind; rather, through the vision of the heart, by the mediation of grace, dear ones see one another there where love itself resides.

And so, sending greetings to Your Piety, which is most full toward me, as far as I can judge from my own mind, I beg with every kind of entreaty: if you repay us with equal affection, if you love us with a like love, if our love is at work at all in your inmost being, if our affection has reached the very marrow of your heart, if love has tamed you for me with the sweetness of its power as it has tamed me for you, so that you can neither resist its command nor wish to, then come quickly, longing, to your longing brother. Hasten this kindness, both to pay the debt you promised and to soothe our mutual affection, for when we are face to face we shall give each other equal joy in seeing and talking with one another, and if you love as you are loved, as much will be repaid by me to your love as you yourself bestow on mine. Nor should you fear the fatigue of the journey, for, as the poet said, “love has conquered the hard road,” and, according to our apostle, love “bears all things,” “does not seek its own,” and “never fails.” The mild weather of autumn, too, suits the longing traveler well, together with love, provided that the heat of the past summer kindles that love and the cold of the coming winter does not quench it.
XI. Another letter of the lord Ruricius.

When you have read my letter through, you may be surprised that I wrote to your reverence as a brother, since this suits neither our age nor our rank: you are older than I am in years, but lower in rank. So if we had looked to your long life, by God's favour, or to our office, we ought to have written either to a father or to a son. But the holy apostle John too, in his epistle, writes to one and the same people as fathers, as young men and as children, saying: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you have known the Father.” By this distinction of words he points not to the age of the outer man but to the quality of the inner. Insofar as we advance in the knowledge and love of God, we are without doubt called fathers. Insofar as we fight manfully against the adversary, who prowls like a lion seeking whom he may devour, we are recognized as young men. But insofar as we give ourselves up to sloth and idleness, and through weakness of faith fail to walk the way of the commandments, and rise too sluggishly, as if from sleep, out of our absorption in worldly affairs to contemplate and fulfil the divine precepts, we are most rightly counted among children for our frivolity.

This is why the apostle Paul admonishes the negligent man: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and you will touch Christ,” or “Christ will give you light.” And when the Lord in the gospel was told by those standing around him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are seeking you, wishing to see you,” he answered: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” And pointing to the apostles who followed him: “Are they not those who do the will of my Father?” For we can be called the mother of Christ when we carry Christ in our heart. Holy Mary herself, who conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin and remained a virgin, conceived our Lord not through a man's embrace but with faith as her bridegroom. And we become his brothers when we so order, support and adorn our life with every kind of virtue that we can be heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. Who can doubt that if we become heirs of God the Father, we can most rightly be called brothers of Christ as well, since he adopts us? He formed us as his own, redeemed us as strangers, chose us as servants and took us up as sons. He forms us by his power, redeems us by his passion, chooses us in his foreknowledge and takes us up by his grace. Yet we are sons by adoption, he alone is Son by nature. To call us back to the same blessedness from which we had fallen, he never ceased to be what he was, yet he willed to be what he was not, so that the Word became flesh, and so that, while the Creator came down into the lowliness of the creature, the creature might rise up to the height of the Creator.

So it comes about that divine things are shared with humanity and human things partake of divinity, as the apostle says: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.” Hence the same teacher, writing to the Corinthians, says: “From now on, therefore, we know no one according to the flesh. Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him so no longer,” because, now that bodily weakness has ceased in him, he is believed to be wholly in divine power. And so, according to the same apostle, since we are all one in Christ, we are most rightly called brothers, because one womb, that of the sacred font, brought us forth, and the same breasts of mother Church nursed us, with the Spirit giving us life. At the same time I wrote “brother” because I learned that, by God's favour, you have turned your soul from the affairs of the world to eternal blessedness, and have become an imitator of that merchant in the gospel who sold all he had and bought the most precious pearl, or of the man who found a treasure in a field, sold everything he possessed and, with a praiseworthy greed, bought that field. You are not a pushy coveter of other people's property but a provident distributor of your own wealth, holding fast with a perfect heart to a love that is utterly sincere, not so as to sell more sparingly but so as to lend at greater interest.

At this I rejoice and give thanks to God, because, according to the riches of his goodness and power, through his immeasurable mercy he deigns, if I may put it so, almost to go against his own sentence. For although he himself said that it is hard for those who have money to attain the kingdom of heaven, see how he has honoured you with riches in this world and now hastens to advance you into the kingdom. Yet the same Lord at once tempered the severity of that earlier sentence, which the apostles greatly dreaded, by the restraint of his mercy, saying that what was impossible for men by nature in themselves was possible for God in them by grace. That this may be so in you, I urge you, out of the affection of our mutual love, to devote yourself wholly to this work and to be ready for its costs, and to press on as an energetic builder of that tower which the Lord in the gospel commanded to be built, so that your adversaries may have cause to grieve at its completion rather than to laugh at its abandonment.
XII. Bishop Ruricius to the lord Praesidius, exalted and ever magnificent, his brother.

A great many people, trusting that I have much influence with your highness, from whom I am inseparable, not by any merit of my life but by the privilege of friendship, ask me for letters of recommendation to excuse them before you. The duty of my office does not allow me to refuse them, and I write not out of presumptuous boldness but from the discipline of my ministry, since I wish to provide for them comfort in this present life and for you comfort in the life eternal: that they, through your patience, may be kept for repentance, and you, through your mercy, may attain pardon. As Scripture says: “Judgement without mercy will be shown to him who has shown no mercy.” For he who said, “Forgive, and it will be forgiven you,” will without doubt restore in the world to come what he promised to whomever he sees doing here what he commanded. His truth stands ready for us, if our faith in him does not fail. From this you can see quite plainly that pardoning those who are in your power and in misery means forgiveness of your own sins, and that your prayers will be granted what you have granted to others, in keeping with his own saying in the gospel: “With the judgement you pronounce you will be judged.” Therefore I come as a suppliant for Ursus and Lupicinus, who came to me to intercede for their crimes because, as I said above, I am specially bound to you by the bond of love. I ask that you deign to forgive what they have done, first for God's sake and then for ours, and [?], and that you do not put us to shame by condemning them, since they believed themselves absolved when they were brought before my humble self.
XIII. Another to the same.

You were a vessel tossed by hostile and shifting storms on the sea of this world, and I rejoice with you that at long last, with the Lord at the helm, you have put in to the harbour of salvation. Settled in that safe and calm anchorage, you will from now on laugh at the surges of that treacherous, wicked and bitter sea, and not fear them. As you have little to fear from them, so you may now have much joy, because you either look back on them as left behind you or, set on a higher watchtower, look down on them and marvel that you have escaped. It remains for you to keep your hand on the tiller and your eyes always fixed on the stars, and so to spread your sail for the voyage you have begun that no stronger gust drives you out to the deep or dashes you on the rocks near the shore. Nor, according to the saying of the Lord and Saviour, should you, having already put your hand to the plough, look back, perhaps roused by the cries of collapsing Sodom, and so imitate Lot's wife. Nor, having already set out from Egypt, having crossed the Red Sea, whose waves hung on your right and left, bringing you help and preparing destruction for your pursuers, while the Lord both prepared and lit your way, and having taken up the hard road through the desert, should you remember the fleshpots or the onions. Like bodily pleasures, these are known to be corrupt by their very nature, and foul: neither pleasant to use, nor sweet to smell, nor lasting.

Whatever in this world soothes the ear, is soft to the touch or entices the eye flatters in order to catch, serves in order to hold, and lures in order to kill. Whatever pleasure you try to seize, what punishes remains and what delights passes away: the fleeting sweetness goes by, while the conscience that will condemn, or be condemned, stays on. That is why Solomon says: “The lips of a harlot drip honey, but in the last days you will find her more bitter than gall.” And yet he himself, though he had foretold this, fell into it. See, then, dearest brother, what an evil this is: it is committed even while it is loathed, and is scarcely avoided even while it is shunned. So you too, as Scripture says, guard your heart with all vigilance and examine your conscience, so that you do not cling in affection to what you seem to have left in outward appearance. Rather say to the Lord with the prophet: “My soul has clung to you; your right hand has upheld me,” or this as well: “For me it is good to cling to God, to put my hope in God.” Then you will serve God with as much labour and earnestness as you served the world, as the apostle says, or rather warns: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you once yielded your members to serve impurity and iniquity, so now yield your members to serve righteousness for sanctification. When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit did you have then from the things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become servants of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and its end is eternal life.”

Penance, dearest brother, must be taken up not in name but in deed, and carried out not with the mouth only but with the heart. It is true that, as we sin with both the inner man and the outer, so we ought to repent with both. As the same apostle says, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” So let our heart, pierced by conscience, conceive groans, so that our mouth may pour them out in a confession of shame. Let the fiftieth psalm, which is given for repentance and forgiveness alike, be sung day and night with roaring and weeping, so that we may truly and to our salvation say: “I roared from the groaning of my heart,” and: “I acknowledge my iniquities, and my sin is ever before me,” or also: “For I declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin.” Here our sins ought to be before us, so that they can never be against us in eternity, for we read in the prophets: “Tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified.” Before whom are we to tell or declare our iniquities first in the Lord's presence, if not before the devil, who is both the instigator and the accuser of our sins? He urges us to sin, and when we have sinned he accuses us. So let us forestall him in this world by confessing our crimes, so that in the world to come he has nothing to bring forward against us.
XIV. Bishop Ruricius to his most blessed brothers, venerable in Christ, the priests Foedamius and Vilicus.

Although I had received no letter from your fraternity through the subdeacon Contemtus, I have nevertheless sent you this one through him, prompted by affection. I wanted to satisfy my longing and, as the senior, to be the first to open the way to writing, so that in future no room would be left for excuses, and what was really a matter of will could not be put down to distrust and shyness. I therefore send your blessedness abundant greetings in Christ the Lord, and I hope that, as befits churchmen, you will love me not with your lips but with your heart, and will venture to speak of my love as sincere, as I would rather call it, than as a love of old. For if the old love had been true, it would have lasted, and if it had been mutual, it would not have changed. On whose side it changed, our consciences know, and the Knower of consciences knows without anyone to plead the case. I call him as witness to my declaration that I was not to blame for the beginning of the quarrel, and that nothing that was done or said about you has lingered in my heart, for I know that we have been told by the eternal and true Judge that unless we forgive our brothers from the heart, we are not to be forgiven. So you have my pledge; give me your faith in return. In my letter you will without doubt have whichever bond you choose: either a bond of love, which binds and guards for salvation, or a bond of bad faith, which entangles and destroys through guilt. And do not hold against me anything from the judgement of earlier times, for it is my principle to keep harmony in friendship and to maintain strictness in judgement. I am especially glad to have learned that you have returned to full intimacy with my lord and brother. It remains that what his grace has granted for good, your faithful following may preserve in the Lord.
XV. Bishop Ruricius to the lady Ceraunia, venerable and to be honoured in Christ the Lord, his daughter.

The reason I did not send you the painter sooner was this: I believed that with the arrival of the new governor you were taken up with other things, and so alarmed that you could not think about such matters. But since I have learned, by God's favour, both from your letter and from the report of your people, that all is going as you wish and that you are well, I first send my greetings and then dispatch the painter with his pupil, however busy he was here, because I preferred to go without for my own needs so that I might satisfy your request. And since both your way of life and our office require it, I have presumed to admonish your Reverence in these few words: take from his work an example for doing penance and for putting on the new garments of the new man, so that the old Adam may more easily die in you and the One who gives life may rise up.

Just as he paints walls with various tints of colour by his manifold art, so may you adorn your soul, which is the temple of God, with different kinds of virtues, so that of your spiritual house you may truly and spiritually say with the prophet: "Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells." For according to the word of our Lord himself, God does not dwell in things made by hand, nor does he take pleasure in the tents of a man; but he takes pleasure in those who fear him and in the one who hopes in his mercy. And again he deigns to teach us through the prophet: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What seat will you build for me, or what will be the place of my rest? Did not my hand make all these things? Or upon whom else shall I look, but upon the one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?" And the Lord himself cries out in the Gospel: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you," and the rest that follows. And so, sister and daughter most dear in Christ the Lord, you must lay aside the ambition of your former way of life and put on humility of heart; you must lend mercy at interest to the needy, and cultivate chastity not only of body but of soul. So that, with the Lord's help, you may be able both to acquire it and to keep it, you must fast often and pray always. For Adam was appointed both guardian and cultivator of paradise, so that his freedom of choice might have material to work on, and so that the abstinence of frugality might guard what the diligence of prayer had obtained. But because he neglected to keep the fast for himself, through forbidden desire he lost both life and immortality.

Under Zerubbabel, those who had returned from captivity were rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. Since they had to contend with foreigners over the restoration of those walls, they worked with the right hand and fought with the left: with the left they held out the shield of faith against their adversaries, and with the right they built ramparts of good works, as if of fitted stones. Moreover, the men who were building with their prophets worked with their loins girded, which the Lord also commanded us to observe in the Gospel, saying: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning." He is girded in the loins whose flesh serves in the army of chastity and not of lust, and his mind shines like a burning lamp which Christ kindles with his commandments. Since, according to the Apostle, all these things happened as a figure of us, we ought to understand that, as long as we were occupied with the affairs of the world, we were slaves like captives led out of Judaea into enemy lands, serving the Babylonians and their king.
