Therefore, returning through penance to our homeland, that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of all the faithful, we must with every kind of virtue repair what has collapsed, mend what has been torn, blot out the past, guard against the present, and prepare for what is to come, so that, delivered by the Lord's kindness from our former captivity to sin, we may serve not the king of the Babylonians but the King of heaven, Christ, in Jerusalem, the city that is built out of the congregation of the saints. And for that reason we ought to wet our face with tears rather than with baths, so that we can say with the prophet: "For I ate ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping."

We must tame our body with unwearied vigils and continual fasts, so that, exercising true judgment between soul and flesh, the flesh may not dominate the spirit, but may be conquered and serve the spirit. The Lord gave us an example of this when he spoke through an angel to Hagar, Sarah's maidservant, who had preferred to desert her mistress rather than obey her, saying to her: "Return and be subject to your mistress." So, devoted to all these labours and good works, may you be both perfect in your way of life and devout in your confession; and in the kingdom of that Father of yours of whom the Lord says in the Gospel, "Call no one on earth your father, for you have one Father," may you, true to your name, truly shine as Ceraunia among that throng of the blessed and make your name come true. Of this splendour of works the Lord says: "Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify, not you, but your Father who is in heaven." To him belongs both the giving and everything that is given, for according to the Apostle every good gift comes down from above, from the Father of lights, by whom both the will is granted and its fulfilment is supplied.

Penance is not to be obtained in name only but carried out in deed. Penance is no idle name: it is laborious, and takes its name from the character of its work. For one who commits what must be repented of cannot be called a penitent; the penitent is the one who wipes away past sins and stains by humility of heart, subjection of the body, diligence in good works, perseverance in prayer, unbroken groaning, beating of the breast, and a flood of tears, so that he can say with the prophet: "Do not remember our former iniquities" (former, of course, not daily ones); and this: "I have laboured in my groaning; every night I will wash my bed, I will water my couch with my tears"; and again: "I roared with the groaning of my heart"; and again: "For I declare my iniquity, and I will think about my sin." Let our crimes therefore be before us here, so that they cannot stand against us on the day of judgment, and so that, while we are still here, we may be worthy to say with confidence: "I acknowledge my offence, and I have not hidden my injustices. I said: I will declare my injustices against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart." It is certain that as far as you are displeased with yourself over your former way of life, so far you will please the Lord; and as far as you please yourself, you will without doubt displease him who says: "For he scatters the bones of men who please themselves."

And so, like the strictest censors, let us punish our faults in ourselves the more severely; let us in a certain way be our own torturers and judges through various afflictions of the body, so that in that time of just examination the King's sentence may find nothing to condemn in us, whom the discipline of a more chastened life has already corrected here. For the just and merciful Judge does not judge twice for the same thing: that is, he will show himself gentle to the one he finds to have been harsh with himself here in making satisfaction for his sins, and kind to the one he recognizes to have been strict with himself in this life, according to the Gospel saying: "Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it," or: "Blessed are you who mourn now, for you will laugh." For everything done in this world is brief, whether good or bad, as you have already proved by experience, as the Lord either permitted or willed. Therefore we must be steadfast in enduring afflictions for the love of God, for if weeping lingers until evening, joy will follow in the morning. So let us now sow in tears what we may then reap in joy.

Let these few words suffice, spoken to strengthen your faith and to comfort you with exhortation. Though I do not do these things myself, I nevertheless urge you to do them. For I know that a reward is set for exhortation, since we read: "Weep with those who weep"; and lest perhaps you should say at the judgment: "I looked for someone to grieve with me, and there was none, and for comforters, and I found none." But seek out more perfect and greater instruction in the divine Scriptures, from which these words were gathered, if you wish either to complete what you have begun or to arrive at what is promised. To one who seeks in this way the Lord will give both knowledge and strength, so that you may understand what you read and keep what you understand. For the Father of orphans and judge of widows, when he sees that you hope in him alone, will both grant protection to your fatherless children with a father's tenderness and, as Judge, will reward you and lead you to your prize.
XVI. To the holy and apostolic lord, my patron, to be honoured by me in Christ the Lord with reverence and affection above all others, Pope Aeonius the bishop, from Ruricius the bishop.

A short while ago I received your Holiness's letter, in which you even saw fit to admonish me most affectionately for my neglect of duty, saying: "Nothing is more excellent than charity." I strongly affirm that this is very true, and following the Apostle I say that that charity is perfect and sublime which proceeds from a pure heart, a good conscience and unfeigned faith; which, according to the same Apostle, is patient, is kind, is not puffed up, is not jealous, does not seek its own, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth, believes all things, hopes all things; and that is why it will never fall. It is patient, because, fixed on God, it stands immovable against the temptations and storms of the world. It is kind, because it delights in the progress of its neighbours. It is not puffed up, because it is not proud toward the humble. It is not jealous, because it does not know how to envy an equal. It does not seek its own, since, according to the Lord's word, it puts even the least before itself and wins benefits for others at its own cost. It does not rejoice over iniquity, because it knows no gladness except in the prosperity of the brethren. But it rejoices with the truth, because it honours a friend with sincere, not counterfeit, love, and does not mock him with false flattery but celebrates him with true honour. It believes all things, because it trusts in God's commands and promises; and therefore it hopes all things, because it does not doubt that it will be repaid great things for small, everlasting for perishable, eternal for temporal. It never falls, because humility cannot fall, since it is always ascending; and although it constantly meditates on lofty things, it does not presume to dwell on the heights. Although its citizenship is in heaven, it nevertheless seems to cling to earthly things, lofty in its works and lowly in mind, so that it has reason to glory in the Lord and yet is not exalted in the world.

I have presumed to write these things because you commanded it, not out of any learning of ours but because of your condescension. It is for you, however, to instruct us by your words and always to stir us by your example to this same charity, since a love which, before we were acquainted, was begun between us while absent and has always been fostered by an exchange of letters ought to be increased by seeing one another in person, not diminished, and to grow by sight, as it began by speech.
XVII. To the lord, his exalted and ever magnificent brother Taurentius, from Ruricius the bishop.

The affection of an anxious heart demands that even an unskilled speaker speak out; it does not blush at the reproach of rusticity, provided that it fulfils the command of charity, as the holy Apostle says: "Perfect charity casts out fear." For it is far better to love one's neighbour sincerely than to preach perfectly, since many more people in the world are found endowed with the charm of eloquence than perfected in the vigour of love; for just as what is good is rare, so what is eternal is hard. According to the Lord's word, the road that plunges into Gehenna is downhill and well trodden, but the one that lifts us up to glory is narrower and more difficult. What is the reason, if not that many walk the one and few the other? And therefore, since the end of this present age is now at hand and the day of old age is close in every way, as even our shorn hair teaches us, and as is fitting, we should not, in our old age, ponder youthful deeds, nor should the desires of youth reign in a worn-out body and a decrepit heart. For at the time of judgment, at that dreadful examination of the eternal dispensation, when he who is the witness and judge of all mortals will weigh not only merits and deeds but will also sift words and wishes, and, as he has promised, will give some a reward for offering cold water and others punishment for the frivolity of an idle word, he may hold us guilty on account of such desire, if not for the pleasure of a crime committed, then at least for the will to lust; for whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

We ought likewise to observe the same with regard to all other things, so that, having cut away each of the appetites of this feeble body, we may enter the kingdom maimed in such members and yet whole, rather than be cast into the eternal fire safe and yet lost. Having considered all these things profitably and examined them duly, let us, while a respite is granted, turn away from evil and do good without ceasing; let us forget the past, despise the present, desire the future; let us forget in our deeds and remember in our consciences, so that every sin may die to us in our life and live on in our penance; let us now sow in weeping what we may afterwards reap in joy. For the time of this life is the time for work, but the day of recompense is the time of harvest, when without doubt each one will see in the shoot what he now scatters as seed, as one of the saints says: "My righteousness will answer for me tomorrow," meaning, of course, by "tomorrow" the day of resurrection.

These things, excellent brothers, we have presumed to write confidently to you, who are of one mind, at the prompting of charity, not with a bishop's authority but with brotherly devotion, so that by them we might show you, and toward you, not a writer's talent but a brother's affection. And so, sending you greetings, I ask that, as you kindly promised, you send us without delay by the bearer of this letter the book of Saint Augustine On the City of God, so that, while you edify us on earth by our reading of it, you may prepare for yourselves dwellings in that same city in heaven. Yet we cannot reach that city in any other way than by climbing the steps of charity, for charity is the more excellent way, which both unites us to God while we are in this life and, when this life is laid aside, leads us to God. Of it the prophet also testifies: "They walked from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion." Therefore let us here sharpen the eyes of the heart with the eye-salve of good works, so that there we may be able to see God, because according to the Gospel, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Accordingly, the sight of the inner man must be prepared here, so that there its gaze may not be dulled.
XVIII. To the holy and most blessed lord, to be honoured by me with special reverence and affection, Pope Sedatus the bishop, from Ruricius the bishop.

You often blame me and frequently reproach me for not having written until now to your Beatitude, from whom I am inseparable in Christ the Lord. Would that I had the ability to do it as much as I have the will to write, so that the charity conceived in the heart might be expressed by the mouth! But where speech is lacking, affection keeps silent, and within the recesses of the breast it is content with its own awareness that it is not at fault in love, even if it sees that it is not equal in rendering its duties. For it trusts that, just as it perceives a brother's love for itself by inference from its own, so the loving brother can likewise recognize that love from his own; since there is no better way to measure the secrets of other hearts than by contemplating our own hidden depths. For we believe ourselves loved by another as much as we love him.

I have therefore obeyed your request, obeyed your command, to send you writings put together in whatever words I could. If you love us simply, as I trust you do, you will either delete them at once, lest what is dear to you should come to be despised by others, since love and hatred do not listen with equal judgment; or at least you will keep them to be reread by yourself alone, so that whenever the fire of charity blazes up in you with the wish to see us, you may temper your longing by conversing with them. Indeed, so that you might know more fully the sincerity of our love for you, we have presumed to inflict injury on your ears, for we are sure that they desire to hear not so much eloquent things as strong ones, not so much pleasing as true. Therefore we believe that neither the length of our page will weary your Piety nor our rustic speech disgust you, knowing that the more you ruminate on us, the more ardently you will hunger.
XIX. Ruricius, his client, to his holy patron
Sedatus, obedient to his fatherly counsels,
sings his thanks and sends greeting,
and begs him with coaxing prayers, in fear
lest his slight Muse should chance to displease,
too small for the judgment of so great a master.
Gladly run your eyes over this again,
turn it often in your holy hands,
and while you reread it, remember me.
Let your tongue always recall me and sing of me,
let your mind hold me fast, let sleep keep hold of me,
let your lips always sing of me again.
Lay up these verses in your loving heart;
these, as you sit at home or travel the road,
these, as you recline at table among the cups
and the sparing dishes and sweet fare,
shut up in the cave of your breast and the marrow of your heart,
recite them, while your mind sings.
So may he grant us to see each other face to face
and to tell in living words
what now troubles the depths of our breasts:
God, the giver of all good things,
Christ, reigning with the everlasting Father,
[we offering] worthy hymns to the Holy Spirit [?].
XX. To the lord, his inseparable and ever magnificent son Rusticus, from Ruricius the bishop.

Our common friendship brings me trouble from others, and you trouble from me, because those who trust that I can do with you, I will not say much, but everything, take refuge in our little church for their safety. I cannot fail both to grieve at their groans and to yield to their prayers, so that I earnestly petition your authority on behalf of their guilt, yes, but equally for your own advancement. And do not be surprised that I said their guilt bears on your advancement, since the pardon you grant them becomes your own forgiveness, just as the need of the poor is known to be the wealth of those who give. For what we have granted in this world will be repaid to us at the judgment, as the Lord himself says: "Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you"; and again: "If you forgive men, your Father will also forgive you your sins."

From this we clearly recognize that our God has placed his sentence in our own judgment. He, the merciful and just hearer of our prayers, has made our leniency the rule for his own power, so that in a certain way he would have no right to be severe toward those whom he has not seen eager for vengeance here; for what he himself is, he desires us also to be. He is merciful, and he seeks the merciful, saying: "Be perfect, as your Father also is perfect." Every day he grants pardon to those who sin and make supplication, and therefore he also asks forgiveness from sinners. Hence too, by his own teaching, we say in the Lord's Prayer: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." With these words we bind ourselves with the hardest of chains unless we fulfil what we promise, for he also speaks thus through the prophet: "Man harbours anger against man, and seeks healing from the Lord." Therefore I come forward as intercessor for Baxo, who has taken refuge in the church at Uzerche, hoping that, first out of the fear of God and then because of our intercession, you will deign to spare him. By acquitting him you can both spare us embarrassment and win a reward for us.
XXI. Bishop Ruricius to his son Capillutus, greeting.

Your frequent illnesses distress me, though they also seem to me to be a divine warning, by which our Lord, in his most generous kindness, prefers to chastise sinners rather than destroy them, so that those whom the long span of their years has not persuaded, illness at least may persuade to lay aside the cloak of the world and take up the garment of the Church, which is sackcloth, the sign of contrition; for God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. He goes up to heaven who casts himself down to the ground, since whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Hence that perfect penitent also says: "My soul has cleaved to the pavement; Lord, give me life according to your word." What does "according to your word" mean, if not "according to your promise"? That is, whoever, pierced with compunction, has wept over his sins before you in this world, you will lead into the kingdom, where from then on he may sing in safety: "The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper. You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness." Therefore I urge your Piety to carry out quickly, with God's help, what you have been planning, for death does not delay, as the Lord himself says: "Do not delay to turn to God, and do not put it off from day to day; for his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you." And so, while we have time, let us turn to the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world; for without doubt the merciful God grants his help to the one he sees attentive to his commandments.
XXII. Bishop Ruricius to Bishop Euphrasius.

I thank your most sincere brotherliness in Christ the Lord that, when news of our illness reached you, you thought it so important to visit us at once with your letter. In bearing concern for our weakness you show the soundness of your own heart, since, as you yourselves know better, the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned, and whoever visits the sick is strengthened in love. So I hope all the more that you will help with your prayers the one you inquire after with your words. As the letter-bearers return, then, I repay the courtesy of greeting. I tell you that, as the rumor that reached you said, I have been afflicted enough, though according to divine mercy and not according to my deserts. For he who feeds us with tears in full measure has, in his kindness, set a limit to his chastisement because of our weakness, so that our frailty should not fail under the correction of his hand. And so I report that, by his gracious mercy, I am now better. I am sending you a page that brings consolation for your sorrow, and I intend that by reading it you, who have shared our sufferings out of love, may also share in God's name our joy at our restored health. Pray for me.
XXIII. Ruricius the bishop to his most devoted and ever magnificent lord, Verus.

When I had read your Piety's letter, I gave thanks to God, because its account told me that you had recovered before I knew you had been ill. I trust that this happens to you so often because God is gracious rather than offended, since whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives. So this diligent yet gentle admonition shows that you have been taken into divine discipline. A father's clemency would rather correct a negligent son through all kinds of hardships than punish him as a sinner. He would rather draw the wavering and doubtful into his service with the reins of loving restraint than restrain with a harsher lash one who wanders and slips over the precipices of the world.

For he is the most indulgent father of the household, who lays down his life for his sheep. He is the good shepherd, who would rather, full of care, carry the lost sheep back to the Lord's folds on his own shoulders than drive it back with stinging goads. He is the loving father who, when his wickedly prodigal son, the squanderer of the inheritance he had received, comes back to him even late, not only does not hold his earlier crimes against him but even multiplies the rewards he had lost. He cherishes him in his arms, soothes him with kisses, enriches him with gifts and strengthens him with teaching, not so much angered at his departure as glad at his return. For he took upon himself the effects and the affections of all these names, so that, as the apostle says, in many and various ways he might teach us with words, instruct us with discipline, encourage us with benefits, shape us with examples, reconcile us by prayer, redeem us by his passion, give us life by his death, endow us with immortality, justify us by his resurrection and carry us up by his ascension, and so that, having reconciled us through his blood, he might restore us to the Father's grace from which we had fallen. For he is our propitiation with the Father, ceaselessly pleading with his loving-kindness: Father, I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word. Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me. Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing. Every day he cries out to us through his apostle: Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. For whoever loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes and the pride of human life, which is not of the Father but of the world. And the world passes away, and its lust with it; but whoever does the will of God abides forever, just as God abides forever.

In the Gospel he invites us with endearments, encourages us with gifts and urges us with exhortation, saying: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and the rest. He does this so that, bending our necks to his saving precepts as to a yoke, we might harness ourselves to his saving chariot [of humility and misery], and so dare to follow him as he calls us back, to listen to him as he cries out, and not to spurn him while he coaxes us, lest afterwards we feel him as our judge. He himself deigned to forewarn and teach us in the Gospel about that judgment. When he has taken his seat on the throne of his majesty, he will weigh not only merits and deeds but will also examine words and wishes. Anyone whom he has seen here and now neglecting his saving precepts and despising his most wholesome admonitions with a proud mind he will not only shut out from the door of the heavenly kingdom along with the foolish, but will even assign his portion with the unbelievers. Then he will have his lot forever with those with whom he keeps company in this world.
XXIV. Ruricius the bishop to his son Constantius.

I know you are given over to Bacchus, to concerts and all sorts of music, and even to choirs of girls. Still, while youth is boiling so fiercely, it is good to take a breath from these things now and then, and to give your time to the Lord rather than to Liber, and to your parents rather than to songs. So I urge you to meet me tomorrow, which will be Wednesday, at Brive, fasting, and early, though I hardly believe you will do so.
XXV. Another letter to the same.

With God as witness, you had promised me something else: that you would worship him, not Janus. Yet you even want to make me an accomplice in this crime, so that I should supply delicacies for the practice of this error and pour oil on the fire. You know that this does neither of us any good. But perhaps you say: "You promised." How can you have the face to demand my promises when you have broken your oath? So you will excuse me from my promise for as long as I know you are a slave to this passion. Otherwise we may seem to confirm the deed whose agreement we censure, and become a stumbling block to the one for whom we ought to be an example.
XXVI. Ruricius to his dear Apollinaris, greeting.

Because of our mutual love you always deign to care for us, and so I inform your anxious Piety and your pious anxiety that we have taken up a task that has come back to us. It is no small task, but by God's favor a delightful one, and it could profit us greatly if either our understanding kept up with our intention or our talent kept up with our understanding. For a blind man waits in vain for the sunrise. The sun always rises for those who see, but for those who cannot see, its radiance is always covered as if by clouds. I have received back for reading our Sollius, my lord and our common father, whom I had told you I gave to your Sublimity to be copied. Reading him restores my old affection, but because his words are so obscure it does not kindle my understanding. After so long a time, that little flame of love still glimmers somehow with its sparks among the ashes of forgetfulness. Sometimes we stir it with sighing breaths, and at times we water it with tears that are sweet to us. Yet the more the flame is soaked by this shower, the more it is kindled, since the abundance of tears makes the flame of longing and affection grow rather than die. So, if the Lord grants favor to your kind decision, I am eager to go through him in your presence and to become a pupil instead of a teacher. I am neither ashamed nor reluctant, even at my age, to take on a pupil's diligence, provided I gain mastery of the art I am striving for. For anyone ought to learn before he teaches, since a man who has not first served as a pupil assumes a teacher's airs too soon. And what is more fitting than that you yourself should be the interpreter of your father's eloquence? You can bring forth everything he wrote not so much from the parchment of a book as from the page of your heart. You prove yourselves his sons not only by the nobility of your lineage but also by the flower of your eloquence and by every kind of virtue. Nature gave you these goods rather than instruction, since a stream bursting from a spring, though it grows as it flows and gains fullness as it runs, still owes its merit to the source from which it takes its name. If divine clemency had willed him to live until now, he would delight in your perfection now just as he already rejoiced then in your imitation of him. He would see that hope had become reality, and he would not begrudge himself an equal in the one he had wished to be better.
XXVII. Another letter to the same.

Through the deacon Justus I did not deserve to receive a letter from your kind heart and eloquent tongue, which might have instructed my mind and fed my longing. Even so, since I would rather be judged an affectionate rustic than an urbane but undutiful man, I did not let the chance to write slip away. I would not want to lose, I will not say an occasion for writing, but even one for seeing you for the space of a single hour. So I send you my warmest greetings, and I ask that whenever an opportunity offers you always deign to brighten us with your letters, to the loss of neither of us and the gain of both. For what you spend on us in affection you do not spend away, what you give you do not lose, and what you send us on paper you keep with you in your heart.
XXVIII. Ruricius to his dear Ommatius, greeting.

I left your Piety in such a way that I did not withdraw from you at all. I kept you in the same part of the inner man in which I remained with you. I know that I remained there, in a place from which neither the ancient plotter nor any new go-between could shut me out. So I admonish you with that saying of the most wise Solomon: Son, do not forsake an old friend, for a new one will not be like him. A new friend is new wine; when it has grown old, you will drink it with pleasure. So let us grow old in our friendships and be renewed in affection day by day. But if a friend is not to be abandoned, how much less a father, who taught you, who nurtured you, who with the Lord's help brought you all the way to the priesthood, and to whom you may perhaps, by divine mercy, even owe the enjoyment of this light.

But I write these things to your Blessedness not to charge or reproach you with anything. I write as to a dearest son, whom I want to walk without any blemish in this world of impiety, and to appear pure and spotless on that day of judgment before God and his angels and the assembly of all flesh. So I greet your Unanimity and ask that you deign to pray for me, and also that, when it suits us, you think it worthwhile to visit us. Farewell.
XXIX. Ruricius to his dear Euphrasius, greeting.

I am surprised that your Holiness, after the indications, rather than replies, of so many great men, has also sought the opinion of an ignorant man like me. I suppose you did this more out of close friendship than necessity, so that you might not seem to have passed over the agreement of one whom you think it so important to hold in especial regard. So I thank your Brotherliness, inseparable from me in Christ, for deigning to presume and judge of us that there is nothing deceitful in the simplicity of our love and nothing counterfeit in the purity of our truth. I therefore render the service that our unanimity requires, and on the matter about which you deigned to write to me, I tell you that I hold the same view as our brothers. But what needs to be done, or what seems to me most of all ought to be done, I have faithfully conveyed by word of mouth through your deacon, since it would have taken too long to set it out in a letter. Pray for me.
XXX. Ruricius to his dear Heraclianus, greeting.

One who knows he has failed in his duty ought to beg pardon before he dares to greet. Just as facing an accuser is awkward, so pardon comes readily to one who confesses. So we bring our offense into the open, so that we may obtain pardon more easily, since no room is left for accusation once the way lies open to one who laments, according to that saying: Declare your iniquities first, that you may be justified. For the ill will of the accuser will not prevail where the humility of the suppliant has gone first. So, if we have now washed away the fault by excusing it, let us come to the matter itself. We send your Piety as great a greeting as affection can understand but speech cannot express, as great as we can feel but cannot set out, as great as the inner mind, warmed by longing, can conceive but the tongue of the outer man cannot declare.

So, giving thanks to the author of this very love, who deigned to plant it in our hearts, let us pray that he may deign always to guard in us this special gift of his generosity and to increase it continually, since according to the apostle Paul it is the more excellent way, the way that leads to life. For the rest, I particularly ask that you pray for us every day to our common Patron, since, as you read, the persistent prayer of a righteous man avails much. And as our Lord himself says in the Gospel about the man who [?] three loaves from his friend at night, importunately indeed but to good effect, what was refused to the friendship of the one asking was granted to the persistence of the one who insisted. The rest I have entrusted by word of mouth to the bearer, since it would have taken too long to set it out in a letter. So, as the beginning of this letter says, I ask that you deign to pardon my slowness. Farewell.
XXXI. Ruricius the bishop to his son Capillutus, greeting.

I thank your Piety for deigning to consult me about the appointment for the city, although by God's favor you are more than sufficient on your own. Since one who pleases you and your brothers ought not to displease us, you do well to appoint the man whom common consent has chosen. But admonish him to pursue truth, not falsehood; peace, not ruin; discipline, not discord; the public good, not private greed; justice, not plunder. Let him protect the good and reform the accused. Let him not make the wretched miserable but defend them. Let him correct the guilty and guard the innocent, so that by acting this way he may please the judgment to come rather than the present one.
XXXII. Ruricius the bishop to his illustrious and ever magnificent lord and son Agricola.

When I had read your Sublimity's letter, I gave thanks to God, because I learned that by his ordering you had recovered before I knew you had been ill. In this way he took away our anxiety and restored your health. Yet I suppose that this illness was mercifully brought upon you by our Lord himself, who was gracious rather than angry, in keeping with his usual kindness. For we read that the Lord rebukes the one he loves and chastises every son whom he receives. As I hear, this has also been proved in our case. Having set your affections in order, he instilled his own affection in us. And having changed your dress and your mind, he placed on you the yoke of his gentleness, so that, bending your neck to his saving chariot, you may carry the light burden of his commandments and lay down the heavy load of sins.

For this is the change of the right hand of the Most High, when he deigns to make the righteous out of sinners, members of his household out of strangers, and friends for himself out of servants. It remains for you now to prove in your heart the conversion you have displayed in your clothing, and to make this exchange between your garment and your mind. Until now, that old self had blackness beneath white garments. Now, beneath dark garments, let it shine white with the light of good works. For on the day the sinner turns and groans, he shall be saved. But this holds provided that, according to the saying of the holy apostle Paul, just as we have hitherto presented our bodies to serve the world and iniquity unto iniquity, so now we present our members to serve righteousness unto sanctification. We must not be like people who fear God but profess one thing in words and hold another in their conduct, display one thing in their clothing and prove another by their deeds. Otherwise that word of the Lord may bite us, for covering the rage of wolves under sheep's clothing, since that divine eye, as it is written, watches the good and the evil in every place. Without doubt, when he sees someone passing over to him with a whole heart, he himself will come down into that person's heart to dwell there always. Then the one who has prepared himself as his dwelling will not lack him as his indweller.

Let us therefore together give thanks to our Lord for his indescribable goodness. He would rather warn his servants than destroy them, correct them than punish them, and in return for the use of a brief life he bestows the kingdoms of eternity. For the rest, I send you my warmest greetings, and I commend your handmaid to you with special urging, although, saving your kindness, she does not need it. May you always cherish with indulgence the one you thought it so worthwhile to receive with affection. By divine generosity she has made us both her debtors, making you a grandfather and me a great-grandfather by her fruitfulness. I greet my lady daughter with the longing and honor she deserves. If I were able to travel, I would be most eager to visit you in order to meet her. Because of the bond of kinship we always see her in memory with our inner eyes, and we would like to see her with our outer eyes as well. I wish you well.
XXXIII. Ruricius to his holy and apostolic lord, whom I must honor and love more especially than all others, his brother Caesarius the bishop.

Our brother and fellow priest Capillutus has been doubly welcome to us this time. He himself, whom we had long wished to see, has come to us, and through your letter he also brings us something of your presence. As he returns, I have taken care to send this letter, in which I repay your Blessedness the service that love requires. You write to ask why I did not come to the synod as we had agreed when we spoke. Infirmity, not unwillingness, was the cause. You yourself can recall how weary you saw me at Bordeaux, and that was in winter, when I am usually stronger than normal. In the summer I can scarcely bear my usual infirmity even in my own lodging and in cool places, let alone the heat of that region, if I had come. So I hope rather that you will deign to pray for me. And if you want me to come at the other time you mention, if God grants me life, let us know earlier through your man, since I must tell you that your letter has only now reached me, very late. If not for my rank, then at least for my age, I ought not to be notified later than others. Perhaps, to speak less than prudently, I even deserved to be courted. For if the name of their cities lends authority to others, the humbleness of our city ought not to take authority away from us. It is far better and far more distinguished for a city to become known through its bishop than for a bishop to become known through his city.
XXXIV. Ruricius the bishop to his holy and apostolic lord and patron, to be preferred to all others in special reverence and affection in Christ the Lord, Bishop Sedatus.

My thirsting mind often looks for a chance to write to you, lords of my heart. At times, after turning the matter over for a long while, it has found a suitable bearer, through whom it might break a long silence and ask spiritual delights for itself, longing to be sprinkled with the dew of your mouth. It was of this thirst, I believe, that the holy psalmist spoke: “My soul is like earth without water before you.” Surely it longed to quench the dryness of its body, in a sober drunkenness, with that water of which our Lord deigns to cry out in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink. For rivers of living water flow from his belly.” The same Lord also offered this water to the Samaritan woman, that is, to the church that was to be gathered from the Gentiles, saying: “The water that I shall give will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.” A believer may do more than sip this water with the tip of his lips. If he drinks it down as a guest who craves it with all the depths of his soul, he will at once burst out in praise of almighty God and will begin to pour forth what he has drunk. So it was with the most blessed evangelist and disciple who was found worthy to recline on the Lord's breast. He heard the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom and cried out in words that no one had heard before: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

This was the Word who, begotten by the Father outside time, is created in time from a mother, so that the Creator might be made. In this way a certain portion of humanity could be the fullness of the whole Godhead, and that very portion of humanity could by its passion redeem the fullness of humanity. The image of the invisible God becomes the form of a servant, so that the one who cannot suffer could suffer, the one who cannot be grasped could be seized, and the immortal could die. By succumbing to death he would destroy death, and by rising again he would restore life. But what am I doing? I have forgotten myself in my eagerness for you. It is as if I were talking with you about such matters, and I burn all the more fiercely with longing for you as a result. I hurry to quench my thirst as if from some little stream of love, and I attempt things that are unsearchable and beyond reach. Why do I not consider what I am saying, who I am that speak, and to whom I speak? But your kindness, I trust, will pardon what affection commits, because love bears all things.

So I send my warmest greetings to your heart, which cannot be separated from mine, and I ask you to deign to pray for me unceasingly. At the same time I commend to you with a special recommendation a part of my own body, by whom I am delivering this letter, so that through them you may show how wholly you love me. I think they will be all the dearer to you because they bring my portion with them to you. Whatever love you deign to spend on them, know that you are bestowing it on me. If, as the holy apostle says, the lesser member suffers with the greater when it is in pain, then without doubt the greater rejoices in the prosperity of the lesser. So at last it comes about that, when all the members everywhere are settled in peace and quiet, the head exults, since it is the ruler and lord of the whole body. All the members are told to look to this head, as the prophet says: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head.” Another prophet explains these eyes plainly when he says: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he plucks my feet out of the snare,” and again: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven.” Let us therefore raise the eyes of our heart to Christ, and in the night of this world let us lift up our hands to the Lord with fruitful works. May he deign to be our head, and may we deserve to cling to our head as useful members of his body. Then, when we depart from this world, as at Israel's going out from Egypt, we may say to our Redeemer: “My soul has clung to you; your right hand has upheld me.” For the soul will have meditated on this day and night in the prison of this body, so that when it is led out of it, it may not be put to shame. Pray for me.
35. Bishop Ruricius to Bishop Sedatus, holy and apostolic lord, my lord in Christ, and a patron to be preferred to all others in special reverence and affection.

Through the chief physician Palladius I received a letter from your fertile heart and eloquent mouth. With all the heart's longing, it invited us to see one another. But what are we to do, when the different infirmities of our bodies resist the desires of our minds? You are hindered by too much stoutness, I by the thinness of a wasted body. In your case four feet, and those not your own, cannot carry your weight, while in mine even my own two can scarcely hold me up for weakness. So we cannot fulfil the wish we share. God is my witness that, had I been able, I would have come with all eagerness to the synod that had been called. But my weakness forced me to give up the journey I had planned, because I could not bear the air of that region, especially at this time of year. I trust that you believe this, and I do not doubt that ill-disposed people will twist it to some other meaning.

I have explained this as fully as I could and sent you the greeting of a longing heart. Now I have also sent you, if you think it worthy, a horse of the kind I knew you needed. He is gentle and calm, strong of limb, sturdy and powerful, handsome in appearance, well built and even-tempered: neither sluggishly slow nor too hasty in his speed. The rider's will serves him as rein and spur, and he has both the will and the power to carry a load, so that he neither gives way under the one on his back nor throws off what is placed on him. It remains for you to write back and tell me how he pleases you. Still, I presume so much on your heart, which cannot be separated from mine, that even bad things entrusted to you by me (I will not say sent) please you. For such is the force of undivided love that nothing displeases in a friend, when in fact what is bad ought to displease all the more when it comes from a friend. This is why human judgements are hindered either by love or by hatred, so that they do not declare what is right. But you, whom neither hatred embitters nor envy inflames, receive our jests gladly. Tell us fully about your health and your doings, so that the longer we read you, the more richly we may be instructed. Pray for me.
36. Bishop Ruricius to Bishop Caesarius, holy and apostolic lord, my lord in Christ, and a brother to be especially honoured.

We seek chances to write to one another out of mutual love, so we ought not to pass over those that are offered. In this way the word that passes between us may give us a certain share of each other's presence. That word is sent out and not lost, given away and still kept. It seems to depart yet does not withdraw. I send it and you receive it, I write it and you read it, and yet it is not divided. Though it seems divided, it is held whole in the heart of each of us. After the manner of the divine Word, it is handed over and does not go out. It is given to the one in need and not taken from its author. It is gain to the receiver without loss to the giver, enriching the poor without impoverishing the owner.

And so, since my dearest grandson Parthenius is coming to you, I did not delay to send this letter by him. I wanted both to make myself present to you by letter and also to commend him to you. Whatever love you deign to bestow on him, know that you are showing it to me. At the same time I ask in particular that you pray unceasingly for me and for our children. Do not let the distance between our lands hinder the affection of our love. Those who love one another in the Lord, who is present everywhere, must not be thought separated in body, since they are joined in mind through him and in him. Pray for me.
37. Bishop Ruricius to his dearest grandchildren Parthenius and Papianilla.

Since you, my dear ones, went away, I feel that I am only half of myself. I know that the greatest part of me, the inner man, went with you while my body stayed behind. Yet I also see that you remain in my heart, which stayed here. So I greet you, my sweet ones, and I urge you to remember my words. It is certain that, as Solomon says, you can advance in what is good with God guiding you, if you both love the counsels of your elders and put them to use. I wish you well.
38. Bishop Ruricius to his brother, Bishop Peter.

Because obedience is preferred to sacrifice, I would rather reveal my lack of polish than lose love. For knowledge puffs up, while love, as you know better than I, builds up. You ordered me to tell you about my doings at every opportunity, and to ease by my letters your longing for me. You feel this longing not because I deserve it but because of the love for all that is born in you. So I let you know that I am, by God's favour, stronger. But alas, our whole little household is suffering from various ailments. I ask you particularly to pray to the Lord more earnestly. You restored my health by your prayers; may you also, by the protection of your intercession, bring them the help and healing of divine mercy. Pray for me.
39. Bishop Ruricius to his lords and children, the exalted and magnificent Eudomius and Melanthia.

God, who knows my heart, is witness to how heavily your grief at the loss of your child weighs on me. I cannot express it to you, sensitive as you are, in words. The pain of your grief has wounded my mind as if I had lost one of my own dear ones, for by your kindness to me you have made me your neighbour and in a way your kinsman. You often take up my labours and troubles as your own, as your graciousness leads you to do, so it is right that I too should share your sorrows when they come. For if, as the apostle says, the members of one body suffer and grieve with one another, it is fitting for us also [?] the troubles of those [?] we often receive. So we grieve at your misfortune, and we feel that we are present at your laments. But what can we do, my lords and children? We neither can nor should resist the divine will. We must take every care that, while we weep for our sweet children with excessive grief, we are not found blaspheming and offending the Lord. Otherwise the author of death himself may find his opportunity and pierce our souls more grievously than he struck us by the loss of our dear ones. Therefore in every bitterness and grief we must take refuge in God. We must bring all our misfortunes with our whole heart to him who heals the wounded, lifts up the sorrowful and comforts the afflicted. And we must by all means repeat the saying of holy Job: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord.” When Job said this, he had lost ten children along with all his property. Yet neither loss nor grief drove him to blaspheme, as scripture says: “In all that happened to him Job did not sin with his lips.” I have ventured to write this to you, in your piety, out of our mutual love. I could not soothe the grief of your hearts with my own letter, so I hoped somehow to ease it with the words of God. And truly, if you trust me as you would your own heart, you can take no small comfort from the will of Christ the Lord. Since an untimely death awaited your son, the Lord deigned to take him up while he was still such as he taught that the kingdom of heaven is made of. So you may both have a patron in your son and grieve less for his loss, since you saw that the Lord had taken him up. I wish you well.
40. Bishop Ruricius to Bishop Victorinus, holy and apostolic lord, my lord in Christ, and a patron to be honoured with especial reverence and affection.

Our brother and fellow priest Capillutus did not bring me a letter from you to read on paper. Instead he showed it to me written on his heart, where no thief can take it, no violent man snatch it away, no rain wash it out and no age wipe it away. He is a most faithful sharer of your heart and a very talkative informer, and he often and very sweetly impresses on me how you chew me over, so to speak, with the tooth of a constant love. It is not that there is anything in me with which you could feed the hunger of your love, since you are used to receiving and giving solid food that never perishes. But when stronger fare is lacking, you sip our slightness as a cup of milk, so as to temper the desire of a pious and pure heart with the nourishment of innocence.

Yet it is no wonder to find this miracle in your virtue: you love those who revere you, since you are accustomed to love even those who hate you. Besides, you are keeping our two lights, I mean Aurelianus and Leontius, and this increases your love toward us. For their hope and their fulfilment I ask you to entreat divine mercy unceasingly, as I trust you do, and always to pray for us together with them. I firmly believe that the Lord who nurtures them will deny nothing to your progress or to their beginning, since they are still so young. So I send you, in your piety, abundant greetings, as much as the mouth's speech can express, though not as much as the heart's affection demands. I ask you to greet in our name these sweetest goads of my heart, and to water us with showers of your blessing whenever the chance of a bearer presents itself. Pray for me.
41. Ruricius the bishop to his dear Apollinaris, greetings.

My affection for your Sublimity is a violent taskmaster within me. It compels me to serve my love for you rather than my sense of shame, since it does not consider in what language, or on what kind of page, we obey your commands so readily. You force us often to inflict our rustic words on your expert ears, since you want to receive our letters more frequently. I obey your wish; I obey your command. For I would rather trust your judgement of me than my own, because what you command comes from affection, not from authority. And so, whatever displeases you, you will no doubt correct rather than expose. Nothing, after all, is more commanding than love. Whoever gives himself to it with his whole heart will gladly bear the chains it puts on him and carry the burdens it lays on him, for he does not accept the commander's orders unwillingly but carries them out devotedly. May divine mercy grant that the troubles and pressing needs of this time be either put off for ever or held down for a while. Then it may soon let us enjoy the fruit of each other's presence, so that the longing stirred up by letters may be soothed by seeing each other.
42. Ruricius to Leontius, his most devoted lord and brother, venerable to me with every honour.

I thank you for thinking it so important both to take care of me and to refresh me with fresh vegetables, which you know I like to have. In this you have honoured custom and love alike. So, as your servant goes back, I return the courtesy of a greeting. I urge you to keep thinking unceasingly about the calling you have taken up, by God's favour, since God plainly requires not the beginning of a good work but its end, as he says: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved.” We believe that his mercy will grant this. He has deigned to inspire in you the will to do penance. May he also, in his compassion, give you strength as you grow and full remission at its completion. He alone can heal what is corrupted, restore what has collapsed, blot out what has been done, wipe away the past, preserve the present and give what is to come.
43. Letter of Ruricius to the lord Constantius.

Thank you for the delicacies you sent. I can tell you that I received as many of both kinds of birds as you said. At the same time I let you know, my dear friend, that by the same servants who brought them to us I have sent you a boar's back. So, while we feast on the birds you sent, you may fill yourself on a four-footed beast turned two-footed. Still, I would rather you were taken with its flesh than with its way of life. Whoever is always thinking about worldly matters and constantly meditating on earthly things is rightly compared in holy scripture to this animal. For of all the animals, man alone was created and made upright, so that he might keep his eyes on heaven and always look to his Maker, not stay fixed to the ground, ceaselessly busy with the works of the world.
44. Bishop Ruricius to the lord Bishop Ambrose.

The apostle's precepts remind us to give earthly things to those from whom we receive divine things. We are keeping this precept at least in this respect. In return for the heavenly feasts that you serve us, both in your own living speech and through the treatises of the fathers, we have sent you vegetables from the sea. By this we show that we have nothing of our own: we are strangers to the divine goods that you bestow, and the things we send are foreign too. We know that we are exiles from the heavenly [?] seas and rest only on earthly seats. So we ask you particularly to deign to accept gladly these things that are not our own, and often to bestow on us what is yours. Let one gift be given out of affection, the other as a ministry; one as teaching, the other as grace.
45. Letter of Bishop Ruricius to the lord Hispanus.

Thank you for sending us the spoils of the Dordogne. By them you prove your most sincere affection toward me, and we delight in that affection more than in the delicacies. The one checks the hunger of the body, the other the hunger of the heart. The one supplies passing food for the belly, the other gives the mind a lasting affection. So, returning thanks for your love as well as for your gift, I send you, my dear friend, warmest greetings in return. Since you are kind enough to be concerned for my health, I can tell you that I am well, as you in your kindness wish. At the same time I ask you to let me know by the returning messengers where you will celebrate holy Easter.
46. Letter of Bishop Ruricius to the priest Albinus.

The news of our common grief reached me by report, though I was surprised that I did not learn it first from you, my brother. I would have come at once to visit you myself, had not my respect for these holy days held me back. I have sent this letter instead. I hope that by it you will deign to excuse me and console our daughter in my place, since I hear she is grieving violently. Console her both by reasoning and by your authority: our Lord has done with his servant both what he willed and when he willed. Whoever is displeased by the divine ordinance will be seen to oppose the Lord's will. It is truly divine, for he alone who poured our soul into the body can lead it out of the body when he wills. And so this excessive mourning, which seems to come from piety, comes rather from the devil's counsel than from piety. When grief that will not be consoled accuses God of cruelty in its complaints for sending her son ahead through the human condition, she may lose her soul through unbelief.

Let the dead mourn their dead, who do not believe they will rise again. They suppose that the soul perishes with the flesh, and they have no confidence in the blessedness of the soul or in the restoration of the body. But we have the hope of resurrection in Christ, and we believe that our souls are placed in the bosom of the saints, according to the Lord's own promise. So let us turn to him with our hearts and our prayers and take comfort from his promise: he makes those who believe in him live with him, and no one is judged dead in his sight except the unbeliever. Let us therefore moderate our laments, as scripture teaches us when it says: “Mourning for the wise lasts seven days, but for the wicked all the days of his life.” We know that he is dead in body but that his soul lives to God because of his innocence. In the same way, let us who are alive in body die in heart.
47. Letter of Bishop Ruricius to Taurentius.

I thank you for your most ready devotion in the Lord and your most sincere love toward me. Your love imitates the divine goodness: it [?] what it foresees that I will ask of it, before it is asked, and it hurries to anticipate our request with its kindness. It is eager not only to keep this affection that I have for it but also to increase it in me. It gladdens that affection by anticipating it with kindnesses, because it fears to sadden it even a little. So it prefers to offer a favour to someone who keeps silent rather than to grant it to someone who asks. It knows beyond doubt that what is given out of spontaneous kindness has more merit than what is obtained by entreaty. One of these is given to a close friend only out of obligation, while the other is often yielded even to the stubborn persistence of a petitioner. So I return your greeting and, trusting in your kind promise, I let you know that I have handed your slave girl over to your servants who were sent for this purpose. I trust that, as you promised, you will grant her not only pardon but also your favour because of our intercession.
48. Bishop Ruricius to his venerable lord and brother John.

Magnus, whom we both have taken under our care, has now done under compulsion what he ought to have done of his own accord. He has asked for a letter of recommendation to your Reverence, so that, though he has been ungrateful in the past through his own negligence, he may now present himself through our introduction to receive your favour. I agreed to his request all the more readily because I believed, as I still trust, that you would gladly grant mine. So, having offered my greetings, I hope that you will think it worthwhile to receive him because of our intercession, and that, since he has repaid what he owed, you will kindly excuse him the interest on that sum of solidi, not so much for the sake of our prayers as for the sake of the divine commandments. I have no doubt you will grant this, given the life you lead, in which I hear that by God's grace you advance day by day. For you yourself know that the one who will receive the kingdom of God with joy and gladness, and ascend glorified to the mountain of the Lord, is he who has not exacted interest on his money from his neighbour in this present age, but has waited to receive it from the Lord in the age to come. Nor does such a man use treacherous kindnesses to cast the snare of debts that can never be paid over those in hardship. Rather, he becomes the lender and creditor of the One who says: "Give, and it will be given to you; and the measure you measure with will be measured back to you."

Anyone who is unwilling to keep forever what he has chosen to desire is faithless, and unjust even to himself. For though a man may store up much, gather much, and acquire endless wealth by all sorts of trading, he will go down from this world a beggar unless he has first sent his share of his possessions ahead to eternal blessedness. As the Lord says through the prophet: "Do not be afraid when a man grows rich and when the glory of his house is increased, for when he dies he will take nothing with him, nor will the glory of his house go down with him." And again: "They have slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth have found nothing in their hands." If they were kind to their own souls, they would rather entrust their goods to the One who both stands as a reliable surety for the poor and pays the most generous interest. So do not be eager, dearest brother, to get back twofold now what the Lord promises to repay you a hundredfold. There you will need neither dread destruction by the moth nor fear loss to the thief, because our Lord himself is both the giver and the guardian of his gifts.
49. Bishop Ruricius to Bishop Aprunculus.

The affection of our mutual love has required me to send a letter to your Holiness, who are inseparable from me, for that reason alone, even if no convenient opportunity had presented itself. So I have given this letter to your Apostolate by a man of my son Leontius. With it I offer my greetings first and then ask whether, by God's favour, you are as well as I wish, for you yourself know that your well-being is our joy. I hope that when this man returns you will set our minds at rest, by divine grace, about your affairs, since you see how anxious we are for your prosperity.
50. Bishop Ruricius sends greetings to Ceraunia.

Trusting in the most sincere love with which you deign to honour us in the Lord, out of the kindness of your heart and not for any merit of ours, I have confidently sent this letter to your Reverence. In it I wish you abundant health in our Lord and God, and I especially ask that, if it is possible, you will kindly grant us without delay what I hoped for in the message I sent by word of mouth through your servant Amandus. This would relieve us and could cause you no loss, and I shall count it the greatest kindness. In return, I shall strive to repay you with services of my own in whatever you may command or need may require.
51. Bishop Ruricius sends greetings to Bishop Censorius.

I am glad to have received a letter from your Holiness, even if it came only as occasion offered. For it makes no difference whether it is from necessity or from choice, so long as those who love each other converse together, and those whom the distance between places separates in body are joined by the faithful conversation of minds and hearts. This is the general, indeed the greatest, gift that the power of divine goodness has granted us: that we who cannot see each other with the eyes of the flesh may behold one another with the gaze of the spirit. So, as the bearer of your letter returns, I have taken care to send this reply, as you instructed, so as to answer both your concern and our mutual love.

I therefore offer your Apostolate my warmest greetings. As to the matter you wished to learn through my testimony in writing, namely whether Sindilla lost his pigs with Foedamius' knowledge, you should know that I have made careful inquiry among my people where they were. But, as I already knew beforehand, I found instead that your men had been put to trouble and had suffered at Sindilla's hands, and that he himself lost his pigs through his own perversity while boasting that he belonged to the opposing side; whereas the aforementioned Foedamius was in no way to blame toward him. For what he suffered he has no one to blame but himself. How hard I worked in this affair for your sake, so that your men might be released from custody or recover your pigs, you have been able to learn more fully from the men themselves when they reported back, so there was no need to set it out in writing. It is for you to defend your man justly against this false charge, which, as you see from our letter, he is unjustly bearing.
52. Bishop Ruricius sends greetings to his dear Stephen.

In a very few days the kindness of your Holiness so drew me to devotion to you that, although by God's grace I hold you in my heart and behold you with the eyes of the mind, I am still always seeking you, driven by affection. For just as everything sweet seems brief, so everything of the flesh is insatiable. And I give thanks to almighty God for his wonderful gift, which by his ineffable dispensation he has deigned to bestow so generally on his servants: that those who are separated in body are joined in spirit, and that nothing is so distant or so difficult that it cannot be met by the gaze of the mind. Rather, through the sight of the heart, those who love one another behold each other in contemplation of love in the very place where love itself dwells. So it is that my bond with you, which grows in my inmost heart as it is renewed daily by constant remembrance, promises me that your love is returned, and my own heart stands surety to me for yours, since it dares to presume as much of your affection as it longs to spend on you. I therefore send my warmest greetings to your Blessedness and ask you to pray unceasingly to our common Lord that, according to the riches of his goodness and power, for which we confess that all things are possible, even if in this world we cannot see each other more often because of the turmoil and storms of this life and the distance between our regions, he may at least bring us together in that city which is built as a city. The mercy of the Lord will be able to bring us there, and your merits will bring you.
53. Bishop Ruricius sends greetings to his son Praesidius.

Many people, confident that I have great influence with your Highness, who are inseparable from me, not through any merit of my life but through the privilege of friendship, ask us for letters of recommendation to excuse them before you. We cannot refuse these, as our office requires; not from presumptuous boldness, but from the duty of our ministry. For we wish to provide for them comfort in this present life, and for you the comfort of the life eternal, so that they through your patience may be spared for repentance, and you through mercy may attain pardon. As Scripture says: "Judgement without mercy will be shown to the one who has shown no mercy." For he who said, "Forgive, and you will be forgiven," will without doubt restore in the future what he has promised to the one whom he sees doing here what he has commanded. His truthfulness is ready for us, if only our faith in him does not fail. From this you can see most clearly that the release of your unfortunates is the forgiveness of your sins, and that what you grant to others will be granted to your prayers, according to his own saying in the Gospel: "With the judgement you pronounce you will be judged." Therefore, on behalf of Ursus and Lupus, who came to me to intercede for their crimes because, as I said above, I am bound to you in a special way by the bond of love, I come to you as a suppliant. I ask you to kindly forgive what they have done, first for God's sake and then for ours, and not to put us to shame by condemning those who believed themselves already acquitted the moment they were brought before my lowliness.
54. Bishop Ruricius sends greetings to his son Rusticus.

Beyond your usual and proven affection, you also deign to show us kindness, taking from your own use to provide for our expenses. For I have learned from your servant's report that you had ordered that delicacies from your share of the fishing in the Vézère be supplied to us. So, having offered my greetings, I give you very many thanks, and I beseech the divine mercy that, for the honour you pay us out of fear of him, he may grant you happiness in your present days and bestow on you blessedness in the days to come.
55. Ruricius sends greetings to Bishop Aprunculus.

Just as I received with joy the letter of your Holiness through the venerable Elogius, so I have gladly sent this one with him on his return. In it I pay your Apostolate the greeting I owe, and at the same time I ask you to pray for us and especially to beg our common Lord that we may at last be found worthy to come together and see one another. Then the love which, as the Lord foretold, has grown cold in our hearts through absence (which is worse) may be stirred up again in its slumbering ashes by our presence, and by living voices, like fresh breaths of wind, the fire of our old love may be rekindled. And may that fire, after the manner and power of the fire which the Lord sent upon the earth, burn up the thorns of our negligence and sloth by the force of its mighty nature, and light up the darkness of our sleeping heart.
56. Another letter of Ruricius to the same bishop.

The persistence of petitioners makes up in us for the duty of our shared friendship, so that what we ought to do out of the affection of mutual love we do at the command of an outside necessity, granting to another's request what we know we owe to our own love. This exchange of letters ought to be a joy, springing from the goodwill of close friendship, not wrung from us by the misfortune of someone in distress. Yet since we neglect the grace of writing of our own accord, we should at least not pass up the occasion when it is thrust upon us. So I have given this letter to our brother and fellow presbyter Maxentius, whom our brother commended to us in his own letters. With it I offer my greetings and, as he asked, introduce him to your Apostolate, for he says he has acquaintances and friends there who can present him more fully to your Blessedness in person, so that their testimony may be believed where perhaps his own assertion is not.
57. Again to the same.

Our sons Ommatius and Eparchius have sent me a letter full of tears and lamentation, earnestly begging me to intercede with your Holiness for the ignorance of our son Eparchius himself, trusting that, because of our mutual love, you would refuse us nothing. I have therefore sent our presbyter Eusebiolus to your Piety about this matter. Through him I send my warmest greetings and ask that, once the aforementioned man has been sufficiently admonished, as is fitting, you will kindly pardon his error in answer to our plea. For just as guilt ought not to be remitted for one who foolishly and faithlessly persists in defending his sin until he acknowledges his offence, so acknowledgement of sin ought to bring pardon to the one who confesses it. Sincere confession of a fault is the remedy for wrongdoing, and there is no place left for public punishment where the guilty man is punished by the torment of his own conscience.
58. Another letter of Ruricius to the same.

The day before I received your Holiness's letter I had sent my fellow presbyter to your Brotherliness about the same matter on which you wrote to me, as you will be able to learn from his own report. For not only our son Eparchius himself but also his brother had tearfully begged me by letter to come to your Apostolate as an intercessor, and I agreed, moved by his confession of guilt, his plea for pardon, and the affection of kinship, since I did not think you were going to write to me about the matter. But since you have deigned, out of the love which by God's grace exists between us, to consult my lowliness and ask me to tell you, preferably by letter, whether your severity was just, let my lord know that I approve, praise, and greatly admire what you have done. For while you inflicted pain on one man, who was not beyond hope, through the admonition of the spiritual sword in order to restore him to health, you brought healing to many who were sick.

For many in the Church who cannot be cured by words are healed by example. It remains for mercy to follow severity, so that you may receive with a father's gentleness the one you have rebuked with a bishop's authority. Following [?] that father in the Gospel, whom we ought to follow and imitate in all things, who not only mercifully granted pardon to the son who had squandered his father's substance and confessed his wrongdoing, but also gladly restored him to his former favour, let us too grieve with the fallen and help the broken; let us embrace the one who returns and rejoice over the one who is found. I am sure that your Apostolate did this precisely so that you might shut out from his mother for a little while a son who was ailing, in order to restore him to her sound after a short time, and might sadden for a time the one over whom you long to rejoice forever.
59. Bishop Ruricius sends greetings to his son Severus.

In excusing yourself you rebuke our negligence and laziness, and we recognize that we are in your debt for your kindnesses and services. But I know that you do this out of the sincere and perfect love with which you love us, for what you give us seems too little to your love, since you long to spend yourself wholly on us every day. Yet the goodwill of a ready heart would be more than enough for us, even if constant attentions were lacking. So, having offered my greetings, I give your Piety the most abundant thanks, because you not only keep but even surpass the affection that your father, of blessed memory, had for me.
60. Bishop Ruricius sends greetings to his son Storachius.

I give and feel abundant thanks to your Piety for letting us learn of our servants' negligence, while your kind affection supplied the suitable means of transport that the cunning enemy had taken from us. The Lord allowed him to inflict this on us for a time so that he might test both our patience through the injury and your love toward us through your compassion, and so that, without loss to our own means, he might bring you the profit of a good work through this kindness born of love.
61. Bishop Ruricius sends greetings to his son Vittamer.

Your graciousness makes us your intimates, since what we gladly offer you gladly receive; for a gift proves acceptable and sweet when it is commended not by its size but by affection. This makes us include in our prayers, in paying you the service of our spontaneous devotion, what we cannot put into words. So, having offered my greetings, [?] because I have ventured to send a hundred pears to your Highness and another hundred to my daughter. If perhaps their taste displeases you, they will please you, we trust, by the affection of the one who sends them.
62. Bishop Ruricius to his brother Namatius.

I send you my warmest greetings and hope that, if you cannot come to us the day after tomorrow, you will at least kindly come on Tuesday. For we are on fire with longing for your love, and we too say with the prophet: "My soul is like a land without water for you. My spirit has failed. Do not turn your face away." Do not delay your coming, so that you may quench the fire in our heart which you kindled by the comfort of your short visit.
63. Bishop Ruricius to his son Vittamer.

I thank your Highness, so very gracious toward me, for setting our minds at rest about your affairs and your well-being through your diligent letters, since you know that by God's grace we are anxious about them, as the bond of friendship requires. So with this letter I return to your Nobility the courtesy of greeting, and let you know that I have sent it to you from Decaniacum. And, as I tell you that by divine favour I am safe and well, which I trust will please you, the Lord will grant that I may soon return from here and be worthy to come into your sight, so that the longing you have stirred by your kindness you may satisfy by seeing me in person.
64. Bishop Ruricius to his brother, Bishop Clarus.

For the love that you show me, not because of my merits but out of the goodwill of your heart, I cannot, I will not say repay your Apostolate with kindnesses in return, but cannot even express in words the thanks you deserve. Still, by letter I pay the greeting I owe, and through the conversation of this page I send you a part of my heart, in which I have eagerly received my affection for you. At the same time I beg you to pray to our common Lord that he may soon let us enjoy the fruit of each other's presence, and that those whom he has bound together by the prompting of his inspiration he may also unite by the sight of one another's faces, so that the longing kindled in us by your words may be quenched by seeing you. As for the columns, I thank you, and as you instructed, since I cannot send wagons there now because winter is approaching, I shall send them after holy Easter, God willing. As for the smaller ones, as you asked by word of mouth, I tell you that I need at least ten, if they can be found. But if the Lord grants that all goes well, I shall send a man to you before I send the wagons.
65. Bishop Ruricius to his brother, Bishop Volusianus.

Our old and deep-rooted love has been so blotted out by long forgetfulness, which is worse, partly, I must confess, through our own negligence, partly through the necessity of the times, and partly through bodily infirmity, that, having utterly forgotten each other, we seek each other out neither with any mutual services nor even with letters. I am surprised that your Nobility sends me a letter as though to a son, when, without any regard for religion or kinship, the wrongs done to us please you so much that you will not avenge them. Indeed, had I not considered the standing of my person and my office, I would have sent the bearer of your letter back to you in the same state as that to which my people have been reduced, not by your matron but by a mistress far too insolent and unbridled. If you have put up with her ways for so long, to the detriment of your reputation, whether willingly or out of necessity, you should know that others are neither willing to bear them nor content with them. As for your writing that fear of the enemy has made you sluggish, a man who is used to putting up with an enemy at home ought not to fear one from outside.
Letters written to Ruricius.
1. To his lord, exalted in the honour of religion and to be magnified for the merits of his faith, his son Ruricius, from Graecus.

Thanks be to the Lord that the merit of your faith, as it advances in devotion, so also grows in works. You anticipate the needs of those in hardship with your care, cherish them with your kindness, and support them with your humanity. By these things, as the Apostle says, being fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, rejoicing in hope, you are acquiring for yourself the divine rewards of eternal life. But in your Highness these things are nothing new, for your heart, as it is full of the fear of God, is equally full of love.
