I mean the love that alone gains by being used and grows by being given away, knowing what it pays out yet feeling no loss. For when it is paid out, it is not spent, but rather increases as it is laid out; and by its grace the receiver is so enriched that the giver is not diminished. In the likeness of God, it gives what it has and still has what it has given.
2. To his lord, most blessed and most reverend, and to be honoured by me above all with the reverence due to him, his patron in Christ, Bishop Ruricius, from Victorinus.

Although I was granted the sight of your Beatitude only for the briefest time and only once, yet at that first meeting, when I came to know and behold you, you so watered my senses from the purest fountain of your kindly heart that, though I do not receive the precious gifts of your conversation, I still possess your presence in the depths of my mind. So even if no outward occasions come to renew my longing, I find them within myself whenever I recall your grace. For it is not right that a good which has been poured into one's very marrow should look for increase only from aids that come from outside. Hence the love that grows sweet in my heart, renewed by constant remembrance of you, promises me your love in return. And so my affection for you comes forward as surety for your feelings toward me, and in a way the awareness of my inner self stands beside me as a witness to your love for me in turn; and when I ask how much I may presume upon you, I question my own mind, which burns toward you with the whole ardor of love. Therefore, in offering my greeting and asking your intercession on behalf of the bearer of this letter, I give you thanks that fall short of what is due. This unhappy man was tossed through exile in various regions to win his wife's release, and her death, following immediately upon her ransom, made all his toil vain; now a father's anxiety torments him again over the ransom of his daughter. Be pleased, then, to have him accompanied by your letters, so as to heap up the abundance of your reward.

May the merciful Lord deign to multiply your Beatitude, whom I revere, both in years and in merits, for the advancement and adornment of his Church, my most blessed and most reverend lord, my patron in Christ, whom I am bound to honor with singular and due reverence.
3. To the holy and most blessed lord, the father worthy of all my reverence and honor, my lord and patron in Christ, Bishop Ruricius, from Taurentius.

The letter of your Holiness has fed me with spiritual food and roused me to the hope of things to come, and words radiant with prophetic brightness have shone with purest light to scatter the darkness of errors. I recognize in it an affection full of love, and I embrace the sincerity of your loving rebuke. You show eloquence in your words, perfection in your examples, grace in your counsel, diligence in your duty, constancy in the truth, truth in your admonition, and knowledge in doctrine. You have recalled to me the ancient interpreters of the Scriptures and expounders of the divine books, names I revere: Cyprian, Augustine, Hilary, Ambrose—some blooming with the flower of eloquence, some spiritual in revealing hidden things, some gently soothing the minds of the unlearned, some fighting in defense of the faith.

We find fault with the age gone by, because these present times did not bring forth those men so worthy of admiration. Certainly younger men had sought out the teaching of those who taught before them. As for me, I recognize my age not from the husk of whitening hair, nor, as your Beatitude borrowed from a secular author, from the color of a whitening beard; for even if there were an error in the reckoning, I would feel the years of one growing old from the sluggishness of my limbs as my illness increases. But with all humility of prayer I beg you to make supplication in your holy prayers for the correction of my conduct, for the inspiring in me of a desire to repent, and for the favor of our Lord. Then you who point out the steep path, to be climbed with toil, so that we may avoid the downward slope of that road which leads to ruin, may also obtain for me the entry upon good works and the fruit of devout amendment—not by the lash of discipline, but by the medicine of forgiveness and the gentleness of mercy. Win this reward too for yourself: for you owe the Lord interest on the treasure that was entrusted to your faithfulness and received by you at his commission. Win back those who despair, rebuke the negligent, shake awake those given over to the sleep of idle security, rouse the sluggish. It befits the good shepherd to carry the lost sheep back on his shoulders, and to shut those for whom the wolf lies in wait within more secure folds.

As you instructed, I have found the holy Augustine, which I had believed to be with our common son, the priest Rusticus. My zeal deserves your admiration: I, who until now did not know what works it contained, have now at last looked through it chapter by chapter, as I am about to hand the book over. It is a papyrus book and not strong enough to bear rough handling, since papyrus, as you know, is quickly worn away by age. Read it, if you please, and have it copied. And I hope that once it has become well known to you, it will be sent back to me, to whom it is unknown, since I intend to make up for my negligence by frequent reading of the parchment itself. Pray for me.
4. To the holy and most blessed lord, to be looked up to with apostolic reverence, Pope Ruricius, from Sedatus.

I fully believed, and, however laborious it might be for you, I earnestly hoped, that you would come to this business which has brought us here, so that at least through that occasion I might earn your blessing and our common longing might be satisfied by seeing each other. And truly, once my hope of your presence was disappointed, as though cast down from the summit of my wishes [?], the toil that has weighed upon me, my absence from home, and everything that heaps up the sickness of disappointed hope and anxiety all came together in my mind at once. The Lord knows that if my strength sufficed, or the weakness of age allowed me to follow my desires, or if there were animals capable of making so long a journey at such a season, I would not return from Toulouse until I had earned the most longed-for blessing of your Beatitude and of that singular love of yours. But since the things I have mentioned stand in the way of my desires, I ask and adjure you by Christ that your kindness may always keep me present before you. Do not allow love to be diminished by slowness in our exchanges, or clouded by forgetfulness, but pray for me unceasingly, as I am sure you do, and whenever it is convenient, deign to visit your servant by conversing through letters.
5. To the holy and most blessed lord, to be looked up to with apostolic reverence, Pope Ruricius, my special patron before the Lord, from Sedatus.

Our son refreshed me with news of your health and with your greeting, and through him I have sent a letter—one I had not merited—satisfying my longing in this way, if only a page of courtesy might reach you. So I greet you most warmly and ask, by that love which tells me of your affection and kind regard, that you not be reluctant, whenever it is convenient, to visit your servant with the gift of a letter. For I call God to witness that, next to your presence, nothing is sweeter to me than to be granted conversation with your most longed-for Piety, even if only by the favor of a letter. I also ask and beg with every prayer that you deign to intercede and pray for me without ceasing, as I am sure you do. I greet our sons with reverence and longing.
6. To the lord holy and most blessed in merits, the pope to be looked up to with honor and reverence, the apostolic father, lord Bishop Ruricius, from Euphrasius.

I have learned from a faint rumor that your Piety is unwell, and so I have sent the bearer of this letter so that you may quickly relieve my anxiety over the bitterness of the news. For divine Mercy knows that I share both your sadness and your illness, not with the grief of one who sympathizes but of one who suffers them himself. So may divine compassion grant me, for many years, the vigor of your bodily strength and the briskness of full health; for truly I shall feel myself restored only when I learn, the sooner the better, the longed-for news of your well-being.
7. To the holy and most deserving lord, to be ranked above the lights of Christ and greatly longed for in Christ, the most pious lord Bishop Ruricius, from Bishop Caesarius.

While my mind was greatly troubled as to why we had not been granted your presence at the synod, my holy lord Bishop Verus was kind enough to tell me that he had sent your letter to me at Agde by his deacon; yet by some chance or negligence I do not recall having received it. Nevertheless I trust most certainly my holy lord, your brother, and I prefer to blame this on the carrier's negligence. But even though you did send your holy and welcome letter, still, as you yourself know very well, it would have been most fitting for you to send someone to sign in your place, so that what your holy brothers decreed might be confirmed in your person.

But since I knew with what holy, constant, and devout desire you had wished to be present, I explained your wish and holy intention to all your brothers, so that we neither could nor should hold anything against your Piety. And although we did not have your welcome presence, we felt that we had been granted the support of your prayers. And so, with this letter, I greet you most warmly, with the affection and honor that are due, and ask that you commend me to the Lord by your holy and illustrious prayers and merits. At the same time I inform your Piety that, since your son Eudomius desires to bring this about if he can, we may, with Christ's favor, hold a synod at Toulouse next year, where he also wishes, if possible, the bishops of Spain to assemble. Pray, therefore, that the Lord may deign to grant fulfilment to so holy a desire of his.

My holy and dearest brother, the priest Capillutus, who loves you and sings your praises, I commend to your Holiness as warmly as I can, and I give you great and abundant thanks on his behalf, since, as he himself declared, your devout and sincere goodwill spent itself on him so lavishly that no one could describe it. Now, therefore, since he has sought out your Piety, burning with longing for you, I judged it fitting to send a letter from my humble self by him; and on his return, if Christ allows, I long to be granted a letter from you as a heavenly gift. Pray for me.
8. To the holy and most blessed lord, to be looked up to with apostolic reverence, lord and Pope Bishop Ruricius, from Bishop Sedatus.

I have received the horse you sent by our brother the priest, loaded with the magnificent trappings of your words: worthless in life, precious in your letter; a horse that moves when dug with the spurs or driven with blows, yet makes no progress at all; most hideous in shape, most shabby in color, softer than feathers, lazier than statues, terrified of solid objects, and not afraid—only from habit, I believe—of shadows alone; a runaway when let loose, immovable when mounted; standing still on the level, collapsing on rough ground; one that cannot be held and cannot walk. Before I saw him, while I was rereading your letter, I believed him to be of the race of those that crafty Circe bred by stealth, bastards from a mare she had slipped in.

I thought he would be hot-spirited and fierce in the race, that when he was led out he would breathe fire from flaring nostrils, strike the plains with solid hoof, and outrun the winds and rivers in speed. For such was the promise made to me by the most splendid language of your letter. I also believed that two strong men would have to hold him back, champing at the bit and grinding the iron with his teeth, so that he should not break away. Nor was I wrong: some were dragging him, others pushing, and several beating him. When I saw him brought out in this way, I wished that you would always send your dear ones gifts as they really were, not as my letter describes them. Yet since you have left me nothing to say in praise of the gift you sent, lest altogether ... [?]
